EXTERNAL AID
subsubtopic: REDUCTION IN DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. The June 28 budget calls for a reduction in development assistance for other countries by $75 million this year and $100 million next year. The government rationalizes this cut in badly needed aid by claiming that we will continue to allocate the same percentage of our gross national product since our GNP has also declined. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo):
That the government recognize that development assistance must have priority, that it restore the $175 million it slashed, and that it take immediate economic action to stimulate growth in our own economy instead of using a falling GNP as an excuse for cutting aid.

CANADA POST CORPORATION
subsubtopic: DELIVERY OF REGISTERED LETTERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are suffering generally from a crisis of confidence and nowhere is this more evident than in the loss of confidence and absolute frustration with our postal service. This is one of a litany of horror stories. A constituent of mine, Mr. Colwell of Barrie, mailed a most important registered letter at a cost of $2.15 on Saturday morning, July 3, 1982, to Toronto, the supreme distance of 50 miles. Post Office officials guaranteed Monday morning delivery. The letter was finally delivered at 11.30 a.m. on Wednesday, July 7, 1982, only after a pressing phone call. Therefore, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I move seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the cost of each registered letter not delivered within 48 hours be deducted from the salary of the president of Canada Post and perhaps he will recognize the plight of Canadians with regard to their postal service.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I direct my question to the minister responsible for the status of women. speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-125, to provide supplementary borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before outlining the main aspects of Bill C-125 which requires additional borrowing authority for the current year, 1 should like to take advantage of this opportunity to elaborate on the government's financial requirements as they appear in the context of the last budget.
Many people were surprised at the size of the deficit we forecast in the last budget. At this time I should like to dispel a number of concerns that have been made known to us in this regard. 1 am also anxious to correct a misinterpretation that has been spread about following the announcement of these forecasts, that the government extended its programs in a period when austerity is essential.
I believe it is important that Canadians get a true picture of the facts in this matter and that they realize that the government has allotted itself just one additional discretionary expenditure since the November budget. This was the sum of
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
$400 million allotted to direct job creation and the extension of variable entrance requirements for unemployment insurance benefits.
In view of the present circumstances, I believe that Members of Parliament will agree with me that this is not an extravagant expenditure. The government chose to maintain a reasonable attitude by calling for solidarity and sharing by all Canadians in order to be able to provide some assistance to the unemployed, home owners and businesses in difficulty. The government is calling for moderation and discipline to steer the economy back to recovery so that soon everyone can benefit from the growth in permanent jobs and the improvement in real incomes.
Then why has the government's deficit grown to such alarming proportions? The answer is relatively simple. The deficit of some $10 billion forecast in the November budget was based on the expectation that the economy would slow down somewhat. Growth expressed in real terms was expected to drop from 3.6 per cent for 1981 to only 2.2 per cent for 1982. However, the slowing in economic activity was far more serious than expected and, in this respect, the government's forecasts were no different from those made by private organizations or other public institutions. We are now expecting a definite decline in economic activity or, in other words, a negative growth rate of 2 per cent. In plain language, everyone guessed wrong, including the government. The extent of the recession has considerably aggravated the financial situation facing the government. The decline in production, employment and income, all of which is due to the recession, has resulted in a loss of revenue for the government of about $4.5 billion. A drop in international oil prices and the reduction in certain energy-related taxes announced recently in the National Energy Program Update have cut an additional $1.6 billion from the budgetary revenues forecast.
Finally, adjustments to the November budget measures also reduced estimated revenues by about $300 million. Thus, because of a weakening in the economy, we have a $6.4 billion decline in revenue.
The recession has also had a major impact on government expenditures. High interest rates have increased public debt charges by $1.1 billion. Energy-related expenditures, which were carried forward from last year, added another $1.1 billion to expenditures for the present fiscal year. Furthermore, the total outlays target was increased by about $300 million to accommodate a number of employment-related initiatives and by another $160 million to allow for the impact on fiscal transfers to the provinces. These and some other minor upward

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
adjustments to the outlays target were partially offset by reductions of $280 million in planned spending within the Energy envelope following the National Energy Program Update. The net effect of all these factors is to increase total outlays by $2.6 billion over the November budgetary forecasts.
Mr. Speaker, the $2.6 billion increase in projected expenditures plus the $6.4 billion decline in government revenues add up to a total of $9 billion, and that is why the $10.5 billion deficit forecast in November has had to be revised upward to $19.5 billion. This, in turn, means a substantial increase in the government's financial requirements, which have risen from $6.6 billion to $17.1 billion. One of the main components of the increase in financial requirements is the roughly $2 billion increase in unemployment insurance payments. Mr. Speaker, 1 believe that, in the light of this information, Canadians will understand that the increase in the government's deficit or its expenditures is in no way due to a voluntary act or lack of control by the government. In fact, I indicated that the $2.6 billion increase in expenditures was to cover areas that are of vital importance in view of the present recession. The projected increase in the government's deficit and financial requirements in relation to previous forecasts reflects, as I explained before, the automatic response of revenues, the unemployment insurance program and public debt charges to the acute recession we are experiencing today. Considering the size of our economy, this deficit does not constitute a precedent, compared with the deficits our own country and even foreign countries have known in the past ten years during periods of cyclical weakness.
More specifically, if we compare the Canadian deficit with that in the United States, Germany and Japan for this year and last year, we see that the Canadian situation is not much different from the situation in those countries. In fact, expressed in percentages of the GNP, we find that for Canada it was 1.2 per cent in 1981 and will be 4.4 per cent in 1982. In the United States, it was 0.9 per cent in 1981 and will be 3.5 per cent this year; in Germany, it was 4.5 per cent and will be 3.8 per cent this year. In Japan, it was 4 per cent in 1981 and will be 3.4 per cent this year. If we compare the government's present financial situation to the situation during the far less severe recession in 1978-79, we find that the government's financial requirements for both years are exactly the same, namely 4.8 per cent, expressed in percentage of the GNP. As for the budgetary deficit, it was 5.3 per cent of the GNP in 1978-79 and is now expected to be 5.4 per cent. If we compare our financial requirements for the current year with those in the United States, we see that their requirements are not much lower than ours, namely a little less than 4 per cent of the GNP, compared with 4.8 per cent in our own country. Finally, if we make comparisons on the basis of national accounts, we find that the Canadian deficit is only slightly higher than in the U.S., namely, 5.2 per cent of the GNP, compared with 4.8 per cent. Incidentally, when comparing deficits, we must also take into account the relative capacity of each government for
financing its deficit. In Canada, for instance, the personal savings rate is generally higher than in the United States.
In 1981, for instance, the savings rate was as high as 12.4 per cent of disposable income in our country, while it was only 5.3 per cent in the United States. This means that the Canadian government's ability to finance the deficit is greater, percentagewise, than it is in the United States. In fact, in financing a deficit which proportionally-and 1 stress the word proportionally, so as to spare the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) further astonishment-would be the same as in the United States, Canada would have more savings available for private investment because of the very substantial difference in savings rates between the two countries. During the first quarter of this year, the personal savings rate in Canada rose to its highest level ever, namely 13.3 per cent. Although our deficit is substantial, there is a considerable body of savings in Canada today, waiting to be invested in our economy.
Mr. Speaker, the government is still convinced that a substantial reduction in the deficit would merely aggravate our economy's present cyclical weakness. In its last budget brought down on June 28, the government was determined not to add to the deficit and it has achieved this goal. The government was also determined to find ways of creating jobs and sustaining economic activity, without adding further to the projected deficit. That goal has also been achieved. By reallocating expenditures and through tax changes, we have been able to provide $2.3 billion for reducing unemployment and helping sectors that have been severely affected by the recession and by high interest rates. We have been able to achieve these seemingly contradictory goals by applying the principles of solidarity and willingness to share and we have appealed to Canadians to reciprocate in kind. We have asked them to give up certain benefits to help the unemployed and to help troubled sectors of our economy.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the House that the government remains committed to its policy of reducing the deficit in the medium and long term. Financial requirements have gone from 4 per cent of the GNP in 197980 to 2.5 per cent of the GNP in 1981-82. Mr. Speaker, I want Canadians to realize that the same forces that are instrumental in bringing about a cyclical increase in the deficit are also instrumental in reducing the deficit when the economy starts its recovery. As soon as the government's appeal for moderation and discipline with respect to wage demands and other inflationary expectations has been heard, prices as well as interest rates will finally go down. Economic growth will start up again, businesses will be able to make reasonable profits, investor confidence will return and production will increase. Workers who are now laid off will be hired again, and new jobs will be available to young Canadians graduating from our colleges and universities. Government expenditures to support the sectors most severely affected at the present time will no
July 19, 1982

longer be necessary, and as the employment rate goes up, unemployment insurance payments will go down. More jobs will mean more people who are able to pay taxes, and businesses that are thriving again will also increase the government's tax revenues. The present increase in the deficit as a result of the recession will also be automatically absorbed as the economy recovers.
Automatic stabilizers are necessary to sustain income and employment in a recession. They must be allowed to operate to avoid making the recession worse. Mr. Speaker, 1 am sure Canadians can clearly imagine what the consequences would be if a government refused to take its responsibilities in this extremely difficult period and decided to cut unemployment insurance benefits or slash expenditures that provide income for Canadians until the economic situation improved. As I said before, the government's requirements for the current fiscal year will be much higher than expected. As indicated in the June 28 budget, we shall have to borrow $17.1 billion during the current year. Since April 1, the government has already borrowed $3.5 billion, which it was able to do pursuant to borrowing authority granted in the course of previous fiscal years and still unused. However, the balance of the unused borrowing authority will automatically expire as soon as the bill is passed. We have already obtained borrowing authority for $6.6 billion under Bill C- 111 which received royal assent on June 17, 1982. The loan of $3.5 billion plus the $6.6 billion already approved by Parliament add up to a possible total borrowing authority of $10.1 billion, while the government's financial requirements, as I said before, are $17.1 billion. Therefore, a new borrowing authority for $7 billion will be necessary to meet the government's new financial needs. Bill C-125 now before the House is proposing to add an additional borrowing authority of $4 billion to the supplementary $7 billion, in order to provide sufficient room for manoeuvre in coping with contingencies. Mr. Speaker, 1 therefore move that Parliament adopt a new borrowing authority for $11 billion.
Generally speaking, the government requires some room to manoeuvre, over and above the projected financial requirements, in order to deal with any unexpected cash requirements. These may arise as a result of government exchange transactions. In past years, additional borrowing authority of this kind has remained at about $3 billion. Under Bill C-125, the government is seeking borrowing authority for up to $11 billion, $4 billion of which, as I said before, will be a contingency fund, which, if it has not been used by the end of the fiscal year, will be carried over to the following year. Again, all unused borrowing authority carried over from previous years will expire as soon as Parliament has passed the present bill. The bill contains a provision dealing with the government's authority to contract and reimburse loans in foreign currency, a purely technical provision which, Mr. Speaker, has been included in previous borrowing authority bills during the last
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
three or four years. Over the years, Canada has contracted loans and made settlements in many different currencies. Recently, however, this provision was added to confirm the right and authority of the Government of Canada to contract loans in foreign currency. Hon. members will recall that there is before the House a bill aimed at amending certain parts of the Financial Administration Act. The bill in question contains a provision in Clause 39.1 as a result of which, in the future, it will no longer be necessary to repeat this provision in borrowing authority bills.
As of April 1 of this year, we had borrowing authority for $3.6 billion under authority granted in the course of previous fiscal years, and as yet unused. When Bill C- 111 was passed on June 17 of this year, that gave us an additional borrowing authority for $6.6 billion, bringing our total borrowing authority up to $10.2 billion. Between April 1 and June 30, we used $4.6 billion of that amount, leaving us with borrowing authority for $5.6 billion. 1 shall indicate briefly how the borrowing authority for the $4.6 billion was used. We first financed about $600 million on domestic markets. The remaining $4 billion was financed on foreign markets, that is, $3 billion was obtained by using standby credit while another $1 billion was raised through a European bond issue last June.
In the course of the year, government transactions on the exchange market brought about a substantial increase in the government's cash balance which is about $3 billion at the present time. However, the government needs these funds in order to cope with the present instability and uncertainty on the exchange markets, and therefore cannot use them to finance the country's cash requirements at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now explain why the government wishes to obtain supplementary borrowing authority at this particular time of the year. First of all, we want to give hon. members an opportunity to consider a request for additional borrowing authority in the light of financial projections which were updated and submitted in the November budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). We also want to have the greatest possible flexibility in planning the debt program, so as to take advantage of market opportunities as they occur and thus maximize utilization of the various sources of financing available to the government, obtaining them at the best possible rate for the benefit of Canadians. The government finances its requirements through three main sources: marketable bonds, Treasury bills and Canada Savings Bonds. For proper planning of its borrowing authority and debt program, the government must have the flexibility to use the tools at its disposal to achieve the best possible balance of financing instruments. For instance, I must point out that the annual savings bonds campaign requires lengthy preparations and accounts for a significant share of the borrowing authority. Hon. members know that the interest rates of those bonds are set for the first year and so those issues are considered as a source of short-term capital. When the interest rates are high,

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
the yield of those bonds is an enticement for the public, but the government can benefit from the expected lower interest rates in the following years when the new rates are announced. If the government did not have the appropriate borrowing authority long enough before the bonds are issued, it would be unable to make the necessary publicity campaign, with the result that undue pressure would be brought to bear on other financing methods such as negotiable bonds and treasury bonds, which in turn might increase even more the cost of servicing the public debt. Mr. Speaker, hon. members realize that the government's borrowing program will be rather heavy in the coming months. 1 might point out that it will be the responsibility of all members to act in such a way that the government will be in a position to plan those borrowings as efficiently as possible. For that purpose, the government must be have the necessary authority to plan its own financing.
Most of the program must be financed during the nine remaining months of the fiscal year and it will be practically impossible to stagger new borrowings because of a temporary lack of borrowing authority without having to pay higher interest costs for Financing our debt. Mr. Speaker, 1 am convinced that Canadians understand that the higher deficit is due to the automatic response of the stabilizing agents in our economy and that in the extremely hard times we are going through, it could be even more difficult for Canadians to accept drastic cuts in government expenditures to reduce the size of the deficit which is justified if we are to live through the extremely acute recession we are in now.

Is it a fund for some new propaganda campaign that it will mount? This government does not need a cushion, it needs a bottom line. That is one factor.
Second, the June 28 budget contained no economic projections beyond the end of the current fiscal year. The government is asking Parliament to grant borrowing authority including borrowing authority which will carry into the next fiscal year, regarding which they have given no financial projections. It is asking Parliament to grant borrowing authority without giving any indication at all of its finances into the future. That is an affront to this Parliament. No banker outside of these walls who deals with a businessman or businesswoman, large or small, would grant a line of credit to a financially crippled business that refuses to provide projections of its cash flows. No banker would do this, yet that is what this government is asking the House of Commons to do.
The government says that its situation is too uncertain for it to predict. In that case, then, it is too uncertain for us to grant billions of dollars to a government that was 100 per cent wrong in its deficit estimates last November.
I will give the government an opportunity later to reconsider this bill. When the government gets its act together, 1 say let them come back to Parliament then. We are here to protect the Canadian public. We are here to protect the people of this country, not to feed the habit of a government that cannot even say where it is going.
Third, this government has deliberately set up new and secret ways of spending the people's money without any ability of Parliament to control it or even to count what has been spent and what has been wasted. Crown corporations have become the new way to hide waste or to authorize borrowing against the name of Canada, and to do it without the knowledge of Parliament. We know the government's belief in the breeding rights of Crown corporations. It thinks that every Crown corporation should have the natural right to reproduce indiscriminately. That is known as the rabbit theory of government. As soon as those Crown agencies are born they can go out and borrow and borrow again against the name of Canada. Today there is no limit to the total amount Canadian Crown corporations can borrow but there is a very tight limit on the ability of Members of Parliament to look into the operations of those agencies.
For example, does anyone here know the advertising budget of Petro-Canada? Does anyone here know how many people who work for cabinet ministers are having their mortgages subsidized by Petro-Canada or any other Crown agency? Of course not. We do not know those things. All we do is give
them money at the demand of this government. We have no means of ensuring that this money is being spent in the public interest. It breeds the bunnies and we have to pay for the bunnies. This House of Commons should be out of the business of paying for bunnies that we do not want to have running around destroying the Canadian economy.
In Bill C-96, the government proposes to impose even further limitations on Parliament's control. Among other things, that bill would let the government write off debts of any amount through a simple vote in an appropriation act. It gives the government absolute freedom to spend any receipts and any revenues that are credited to a vote in an appropriation act. it lets the government use an appropriation act to guarantee loans. I mention that bill, which is not before the House at the moment, because it reduces Parliament's ability to control spending at the very time that this government seeks to increase its authority to borrow by $11 billion this year and into the next fiscal year.
Fourth, the government claims that it has embarked upon a crusade to fight inflation and to save the economy. That is some crusade. Its ministers sit back in their air conditioned offices asking for billions of the people's dollars and then sends secretaries, messengers and trainmen who work for the CNR out into the battle.
If this government were honestly serious about an economic crusade, it would engage in the whole war, not just one limited battle. It would recognize, as the world does, that the National Energy Program is doing more to destroy jobs and confidence in Canada than the salary levels of secretaries in the public service. The government would end that threat to jobs and growth in Canada right away. If it were honest, it would restore tax incentives to let individual Canadians create jobs and confidence. If it were honest, it would cut its spending, not ask for $4 billion more than it says it needs. Last week, the government called it a crusade. This bill proves that it is a pretence designed to have everyone suffer but the Liberal government, which preaches restraint for everyone else and then seeks to borrow billions of dollars, some of it for unspecified purposes.
Finally, I would like to address the question of restraint. This $20 billion deficit government is so proud of restraint. We know of the waste that bobs to the surface, the $110,000 spent to teach Bruno Gerussi and Madame Benoit to cook in metric. We know about the $500,000 spent to provide free brief cases for public servants. While Canadians are out of work around the country, the government, which has done so well against unemployment, is running around buying brief cases at a cost of half a million dollars to provide free to Canadian public servants.
We know about the $3.5 million spent by the government on taxi fares. We know about the $10.4 million spent by the government on what is loosely called "hospitality". These are only the big ticket numbers. The questions could not get down
July 19, 1982

to some of the smaller expenditures. However, $10.5 million was spent on food, liquor and entertainment. We know about the $12,000 spent to send an assistant secretary to the cabinet to the Riviera to learn French while she collects her $60,000 to $70,000 annual salary.
[ Translation]
It is not as expensive in Saint-Jean or Jonquiere, and people can learn French right here or, if they want to go to France, they should pay their own way.

How much more of this is hidden away? How much more of these little pieces that bob to the surface are hidden away? How many Crown agencies are in existence today on which the sun would have set if we had a sunset law, as the government of this party proposed when we were in office? How much money is wasted because there is no parliamentary control over Crown corporations? Hundreds of dollars, thousands of dollars, hundreds of thousands of dollars, millions or hundreds of millions of dollars? We do not know, and the government is doing everything it can to ensure that people do not know how much is being wasted, because it rejects every opportunity to give Parliament, the representatives and the people, the right to see, to identify and to eliminate the waste which has become a stock in trade of the government.
We proposed a special all-party examination of spending estimates to eliminate waste or to eliminate frills. The government rejected that proposal. We drafted legislation to introduce sunset laws so that, instead of going on spending forever, agencies which no longer needed to be in existence could be wound down. The government killed the idea of the sunset law. We drafted legislation to deal with Crown corporations. The government killed it. It rejects every attempt at restraint, yet it comes in here and demands billions and billions of dollars to spend.

Mr. Speaker, there is something else hidden in this Liberal plan. It is going to raise interest rates. It is going to put one more burden on Canadians who are struggling to pay their mortgages and on people who have to borrow so their farms or businesses can continue to operate. Interest rates are already too high as a result of policies that were adopted deliberately by the Liberal government in Ottawa. Its energy policy has caused millions of dollars, worth of investments to leave Canada. Tax changes have added to the investment drain, and it seems the government is trying to bring about a regular exodus. It was going to take steps to bring investments back to this country. The Liberals are using high interest rates to bring back investments that fled because of their policies. Businessmen are paying higher interest rates because of the Liberals' energy and tax policies. The same policies are making farmers and mortgage holders pay high interst rates. And what do the Liberals want to do now? They want to do something that will make interest rates go up even more. They want authority to borrow another $11 billion. Where is the money going to come from? It is going to come from the people who are lending to
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
businessmen, to Canadian farmers and to Canadians who want to build homes? And there is only so much money to go around.
The government will therefore be forced to compete with Canadians to secure those funds and as a result interest rates will climb higher still. During the calendar year 1981, borrowings by Ottawa accounted for 44 per cent of the total amount of new issues in Canada. Any money borrowed by the government in Ottawa is money that Canadian citizens would use instead to create jobs, set up businesses, keep their farms or build houses. One of the effects of the government proposal is that it will be more difficult for people to get affordable interest rates, and that is only part of the cost Canadians will have to pay for this Liberal government's incredible indebtedness. In just 14 years, the Liberal government boosted its expenditures by 630 per cent. Is there a single individual in Canada who has managed to do as much? Each Canadian shoulders part of the public debt which now amounts to $14,300 for each taxpayer. That is on top of his personal debts. That is the additional price each taxpayer must pay for the profligacy of the Liberals. This year, the cost of servicing the public debt will be $700 for every child, woman and man in Canada. So what do the Liberals do when confronted with such an unacceptable situation? They want to borrow even more!

There is much more at stake here than the borrowing bill. Two deeper questions are at stake. One is whether the government will respect the money that individual Canadians work hard to earn. The second is whether this government, which has recently announced that it is on a crusade-

No one, absolutely no one, trusts the government. It is an open question whether the government can ever regain trust. The only way it can do that is to recognize that economic recovery requires more than wage restraint. It requires the government to lay

aside the ideology of intervention inherent in the energy program, to lay aside the assumption in its tax policy, that the state is always more important than the citizen, and to begin a serious war on waste in government.
This bill explains the distrust in Canada. It is a symbol of the double standard. Secretaries's salaries are to be held at 6 per cent but the government's net debt is going to be increased by over 12 per cent. If you take account of all the borrowing this year, Mr. Speaker, the total borrowing authority this year will increase by over 18 per cent while secretaries are held to 6 per cent.
We cannot approve this double standard. We cannot approve this demand for even more borrowing. For that reason I will be moving an amendment now and making reference to what amendments we intend to move later. I now wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle):
That all of the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this House holds the opinion that the granting of an authority for the borrowing of a sum greater than that amount which is required to meet the government's needs to the end of the current fiscal year is objectionable in principle and this House therefore declines to give second reading to Bill C-125, an act to provide supplementary borrowing authority."
I move that amendment based upon the minister's own admission in this House that portions of the borrowing authority he is using here today will be applied in the next fiscal year. It is on that basis and because we believe that there is no justification on the part of this government to have that kind of borrowing authority that I introduce that amendment.
We will be proposing two other major amendments later and several other important changes when the bill comes back. What I trust this government will do, what 1 implore it to do, is to take this amendment as cause to go back and recognize that until it has demonstrated a determination to practise restraint at home, until it is prepared to practise as it preaches, it has no moral right to come here and ask for billions of dollars more of the people's money.

Until the government brings in another bill that conforms with the rules of this House and takes account of that recognition, we cannot vote the government money while it goes on spending money like a drunken sailor. When the bill comes back, there will be some other major amendments we will want to introduce, unless there has been a dramatic change in the proposals of the government. One will be to cut to $5 billion the amount that this government is authorized to borrow. We will reduce the borrowing from $11 billion to $5 billion. This government has admitted that it cannot predict or foresee its financial requirements for the future. It has introduced legislation to limit even further Parliament's ability to control spending. It has refused inquiries into ways to reduce waste. It has no right to be trusted with expenditure of the people's money.
Of course, government services have to go on. Our action will not jeopardize that. All it will do is keep this government on a shorter rein. This government will have to come back to Parliament if it wants to borrow more money. Then it will have to give us good reasons why that money is necessary. We are not going to pour billions of dollars of the people's money down the hole that this government has dug.
The second major amendment we propose to introduce, unless the government introduces a successor bill to the one before us, will provide a limitation on the aggregate amount that Crown corporations may borrow. It will also limit the guarantees given by government for borrowing by agencies like Canadair

I do not use that exclusively but as an example- for borrowing under agencies like the Enterprise Development Board and for financial rescue operations like Massey-Fergu-son, Chrysler and others that might negotiate with this government. While the government is opening new ways to spend money without control, we must seek new ways to control spending of the people's money by the government and by the agencies of the government.
The basis of Parliament is the right to control spending. That is why we are here. That is why we were created. That also means the right to control borrowing. It is more than a right, it is an obligation of this House of Commons.
If the government were serious about restraint, it could have moved on a Crown corporations bill. There was one ready. It could have moved on a sunset law. There was one ready. It could have continued the privatization program. It was already in effect. It could have moved to establish a special committee to investigate and eliminate waste in spending. It could have moved to eliminate the waste that it knows about. It has done none of those things. Instead, it simply comes back again begging for more money. Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on this bill. It is abundantly clear that Bill C-125 should not be before this House now. As the previous speaker pointed out, the $11 billion is not required now. Even the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) indicated that some $4 billion of that amount could well be carried over until May, June or July of next year.
I am pleased to speak against the spending practices of this government and, therefore, its borrowing practices. Bill C-125 calls for Parliament to support supplementary borrowing in 1982-83, and perhaps further on, of $11 billion. The government has created for Parliament and this nation a terrible debt. Already the debt is expected to be more than $19.6 billion for this year. Public accounts published just last year
July 19, 1982

estimated an astonishing national debt of $136.5 billion. This means that for every $10 raised, in excess of $2 must be used simply to service the debt.
There are two very different philosophies at work in this House of Commons. I say two because the Liberals and Conservatives share identical approaches to economics. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) said that waste should be cut from government. There is no question that there is waste that should clearly be cut back. But there is also a responsibility on the opposition to point out where the major cuts are going to take place. To talk about 6 per cent for secretaries and a 12 per cent increase in government spending places a very important requirement on the Leader of the Opposition to say where those major cuts are going to be. He talked about cutting billions. I would be interested in knowing where the Tories plan to cut. I certainly intend to outline today where the NDP would make some cuts.
1 listened with care to the Leader of the Opposition. 1 could not help but recall his profound statement to The Toronto Star on May 5 of this year when he said: "We have looked for a solution other than the government's, but we could not come up with an alternative. At this moment 1 don't have a better solution." Having listened to him for the last 40 minutes, it is clear that he still does not have a better solution.

speechtext:
The Tories want to know who put the government where it is. The people of Canada put hon. members opposite where they are because they saw what the Tories were all about.
The statement of the hon. member for St. John's West to which I referred a moment ago is at the root of the terror facing most of Canada's electorate. One voter in four now supports the policies of the NDP federally, and three out of four are subject to shift between the identical, but equally dishonest, policies of the Liberal-Tory coalition.
The hon. member for St. John's West also had this to say when he appeared on "The Watson Report": "Our leaders have got to be a little less honest. We are not being devious and tricky enough. I am criticizing us for that." The hon. member for St. John's West is a leading Tory spokesman. The Tories can speak for their own deviousness and tricks. 1 find it sad that the media across the nation are so tied to the observance and analysis of which Neanderthal in that relationship is on top. They fail miserably to provide the Canadian voter with a clear view of the real alternative policies and economics presented by my party in this House.

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Let me deal first with the essential structural problems of Canada's economy and analyse briefly the Liberal-Tory approach to economics as against how a New Democratic Party government would proceed. The Liberal-Tory team has, since 1867, allowed foreign interests a free hand in developing resource extraction projects and branch plants in this country. This influx of foreign capital has done much to develop our nation, but in recent years it has returned to its country of origin or, at least, has left Canada. Literally tens of billions of dollars created by Canadian labour and resources-and in many cases Canadian capital-have flowed across the borders. The United States, of course, has benefited enormously from the use of Canada as a branch plant and a resource provider.
The Liberal government, clearly supported by the Tory chameleons, says Canada's economy cannot be stimulated, that jobs cannot be created and that the number of homes we require cannot be built. The steady state economics of producing the goods and services we require is pooh-poohed by the Liberal-Tory team because they say it is not good for big business. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will not change his high interest rate policy and, as a result, the overwhelming majority of Canadians face the prospect of declining incomes and a series of recessions, with the economy recovering for only a few months at a time.
The recent budget predicts higher rates of unemployment later this year and higher still next year. So for what purposes does the government require $11 billion, particularly when the Minister of State for Finance has already stated the government has no requirement for that money now and perhaps will not until November when Canada Savings Bonds start being cashed?
Clearly, with the deficit doubling from November to July- a staggering jump of some $10 billion-we have part of a ready answer. The economy, which is constructed much like a suitcase with a false bottom, has funnelled billions in recent months to the home offices of the multinationals which face debt and liquidity problems around the world. As Canada's raw resource sectors of mining and forestry wind down, hundreds of thousands of workers are directly and indirectly thrown out of work. Rather than buckle down and use deficit financing to design strong, appropriate underpinnings for a steady state economy which can put Canadians to work for the long haul, these two parties, the Liberals and the Conservatives, will opt to use hundreds of millions to buoy up sectors of the economy which, in my view, have already been relegated to the pages of history.
How many members of this House are aware of the fact that the hydro corporations of this nation are now the largest borrowers in the world bond market? How many of those same members are aware of the enormous advances which have taken place in the field of alternate energy? As recently as this week there has been the patenting of the vertical access water turbine, which extracts energy from river and tidal currents with small head drops. This technology eliminates the need for dams, has only minor environmental effects, allows the free passage and return of migrating fish stocks and does not flood or change natural water tables and important sectors of marine habitat.
Some hon. members, particularly Tories, may wonder why 1 am responding to the borrowing bill. I raise the issue of energy and give such an example for one simple reason: it is these kinds of technologies which this nation must foster and fund, not only to get away from the disastrous economics and environmental impacts of Arctic and offshore drilling, but also to avoid the impending shortfall of liquid hydrocarbons and high costs of using coal and tar sands in the future.
Can we easily forget that it is only ten years since the Liberal minister of energy told this House and all of Canada that we had hundreds of years of oil reserves? This coalition of phonies has us importing oil now at a cost of billions of dollars a year. Joe Greene seriously misled Canada in order to continue selling our oil offshore to keep a few big businesses happy, and he was supported in that endeavour by the Tories in this House. Now this same coalition intends to sell off, with 20-year contracts, our natural gas. They propose contract exports this year of 31 trillion cubic feet, 20 times what Canada will consume this year, and we will be forced to use more expensive alternatives in the future. The coalition intends to sell gas, first, through a pipeline which goes from central Alberta to U.S. markets. That, of course, was supported by the Tories. They said the Alaska pipeline would be built all the way up and that Canada would have many wonderful benefits. The people of Canada will have to judge fairly soon what kinds of deals the Liberals and Conservatives can cook up to support their oil company friends.
Second, our natural gas is to be exported by tanker from the Arctic through the Arctic pilot project route and other routes to Europe, and now it is proposed that gas be exported from Prince Rupert to the Orient. Instead of borrowing to sell our heritage we would be far better served by a borrowing policy which would pursue national objectives by developing environmentally and economically-and employment-oriented- sound projects.
Finally, what Canadians want is an honest government which will show some leadership and not sell Canadians out for a quick buck through oil, gas or other deals. Such deals are a sure sign of small-minded politicians who always go for the quick buck to try to buoy up the economy. Through sheer hucksterism, the Liberal-Tory coalition has managed to lower Canadian expectations to the point where convicted sex killers are the only group less popular than politicians. Sure, the Tories will rant and rave about government waste, and there is government waste. I spent the better part of last week battling with the Liberals to try to get them to release records about international flights of senior public servants from the Ottawa area. Fifty-eight are now known to fly every day internationally, excluding officials of the Department of External Affairs, the Department of National Defence and international trade officials. Some is certainly waste.
Some real waste was outlined by the Leader of the Opposition. However, when trips are chosen by bureaucrats for holidays and when spouses' travel is paid, combined with the
July 19, 1982

fact that not one bit of information has been released by the ministers responsible with respect to those tickets and other waste, it is truly shameful.
However, should this debate on the borrowing of $11 billion be solely on waste? Surely not, because those same members of the Tory caucus who howl about waste never lifted a finger in government only two years ago to set up procedures to stop it. They did absolutely nothing.
What about the Liberals? Mr. Speaker, would you hire an arsonist to study a self-set fire? I proposed today in a motion under Standing Order 43 that members of the opposition be allowed to scrutinize certain government expenditures and, as always, the Liberals turned it down.
We are running out of oil. This is the twentieth consecutive year of production declines in Alberta. This country is even running out of wood. In British Columbia, forestry officials from the public and private sectors admit that we face a serious wood shortage or fall-down effect within the next 30 years. It would take 160 years to replant the naked backlog in areas requiring seedlings at our present rate of reforestation in British Columbia.
As far as the coal deal in British Columbia is concerned, even though we can construct the stacker-reclaimer in Canada, it is to be built in Japan. The boats to haul the coal could be built at Burrard but instead they will be built in Korea and Belgium. The boats for the gas deal will be built in Japan and Korea.
Is it any wonder that we have no secondary industry when hundreds of thousands of jobs are exported with our underpriced petroleum? The government is intent-wittingly or not-on bankrupting this and future generations by continuing with a policy of supporting long-term energy, mineral and forestry exports and, as often as possible, in the raw form, without instituting policies to employ and benefit all Canadians.
Surely the time has come for an industrial strategy which funnels Canadian capital and aspirations into high technology, manufacturing and an employment base that is secure. No nation, no region and no family can survive the kind of economic storm that such a high debt and insecure industrial base provides.
We have a $21 billion trade deficit in manufactured products. That amounts to over $1,000 for every man, woman and child in excess goods purchased outside Canada. It spells the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs.
Why does business not invest and construct the widgets and gadgets in this country? In part the answer is in the way in which the $11 billion to be borrowed in this bill are to be spent. After all, only a month ago the government came before the House to borrow $6.6 billion through Bill C-111. To my knowledge that money has not yet been spent.
In the seven months since the ill-fated November budget, the deficit has climbed from $10.5 billion to $19.6 billion. The
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
same seven-month period has witnessed revenues falling more than $6.4 billion, from $69.9 billion to $58.5 billion. Simultaneously expenditures have increased by $2.7 billion, from $75.4 billion to $78.1 billion.
Simply put, with so many Canadians out of work and so many small and big businesses failing, tax revenue is not as high as was expected. There will be about $600 million less in personal income tax paid this year than was projected in November. This figure may vary widely as more Canadians move to a system of barter and trading of services in order to stay afloat economically. All of this will occur more dramatically due to the fact that personal taxes, for those still working, will be increased by $160 million in 1982-83 by deindexing.
During this same seven-month period, projections for income from corporate tax have fallen by $2.75 billion. Revenue from federal sales tax has fallen by $820 million because the economy has slowed to such an extent. Surely even untrained observers of the economy must note the intention of the Liberals and, to an even greater extent, the Tories.
An article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on April 17 this year written by Peter Cook said that this recession has been unique in several respects and that an examination of the cause of the downturn, rather than its effect, shows it to be a recession deliberately brought about and fostered by government to a degree that has not occurred before.
Individual Canadians are carrying an increasing proportion of the federal tax load. In 1952, individuals carried 23 per cent of the federal tax burden; 30 years later that has risen to 47 per cent. Corporate taxes made up 21 per cent in 1952 and had fallen to 13.7 per cent by this year. That is almost the reverse of what happened to the individual worker.
If this trend is to continue, the Liberals and Conservatives will make individual Canadians carry the full load of taxes by the turn of the century while the corporate sector will pay nothing. If this philosophy continues-despite the glaring evidence of the corporate sector pouring profits and dividends out of Canada-it will lead to a tax revolt across the nation.
Should the workers in the forest industry, for example, pay 30 per cent or more in income tax when they see MacMillan Bloedel, Crown Zellerbach or other corporations diverting profits made from harvesting and selling Canadian trees with Canadian labour to building pulp mills or saw mills in Brazil or Indonesia and not paying part of those profits as tax? It is both wrong and insulting to lay off tens of thousands of those workers and, after years of overharvesting, simply to move that forest-based capital to other nations and industries.
The Liberal government, supported by the Tories in this drive toward extending the recession, has created a need for an additional $1.1 billion to service the debt as a result of high interest rates. The Minister of Linance personally drove home his desire for higher rates by issuing Canada Savings Bonds at 19.5 per cent. A responsible government should have led the way to restraint by issuing low-interest shares in a scheme to rebuild the country. Most Canadians are eager and willing to

speechtext: Tell us about that. Borrow more?

speechtext: The hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) always has lots to rant and rave about, but I do not see him stand in his place very often to tell the House or the people of Canada exactly what he would do.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: You are not here very often.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
He is long on rhetoric and short on fact.
The reason that the accumulated national debt for every man, woman and child has reached $6,000, or over $14,000 for every worker, is that borrowed money has been used to bail out losers, to subsidize the oil and gas companies and other sectors. These so-called investments have not been giving Canadians a return on their money and now they are not even providing employment.
Government waste must be stopped. Government handouts to continual losers, such as the nuclear industry, must be reevaluated. Crown corporation borrowings and many questionable developments, such as most dams, must be stopped. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Tell us about some of your own policies.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: This is what the leader of the hon. member's party had to say, Mr. Speaker: "We have looked for a solution other than the government's, but we couldn't come up with an alternative. At this moment 1 don't have a better solution." That was said on May 5.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: Right on.

speechtext:
An hon. member says "Right on." The Tories have voted to keep the Liberals' economic policies in operation
34 times this session alone. They do not like to talk about it but they are only marginally different from the Liberals.
The NDP has a workable Canadian option. We will cut interest rates. High rates are the driving force of this recession. They are of immense value to the wealthy in this country who are picking up farms, small businesses, homes and real estate at bargain basement prices. They will benefit immensely when they integrate into monopolies or sell these assets back at a future date to the same workers and individuals who originally owned them.
By stimulating the economy and providing full employment, the NDP would generate $3.6 billion in additional tax revenue. A $2.2 billion tax cut to low and middle-income earners through a refundable tax credit would create 50,000 jobs. By negotiating a postponement of the September 1 energy price hike, we would put $450 million back into the hands of consumers to spend in the marketplace.
We would put $2 billion into seed money for a corporation called Enterprise Canada to help Canadian industry modernize and move into the technologies of the 1980s. We have one of the most capable and educated work forces in the world. Private capital has remained in the resource extraction sector due almost solely to government subsidies, policies and profits.
We believe that the hundreds of billions of dollars in savings and assets of Canadians will be self-motivated to join in the task of creating a new and dynamic Canada once we have an honest government. The National Energy Program was a failure because the Liberals changed the rules retroactively. Canadians do want to hold a majority interest in Canadian developments will do so when led by an honest government.
We in the NDP will reshape the banking, savings and taxation systems to put small state of the art technology into communities from St. John's, Newfoundland, to Queen Charlotte city. Canadians want their small communities to survive; they want good, secure and interesting jobs for their sons and daughters in Montreal, Vancouver, Gimli, Terrace and Whitehorse. All that is lacking is the distribution of factual political material in a language that can be understood.
I come from a little community of only 100 people, Mr. Speaker, but they and the majority of the people in northwestern British Columbia do not vote Liberal or Conservative any more. They know that the big business coalition has let this country down. Through sleight of hand and well-practised deception-to the point, I might add, where many of the Liberals and Tories in this House believe that what they are saying is in the best interests of the country-Adam Smith's invisible hand is strangling small business, forcing our elderly to eat dog food, forcing our working class to bear debt, while the big-business elite reap profits.
We would put $500 million into the construction of social and adequate housing, creating 110,000 jobs. We would put $260 million into programs of reforestation and fisheries
July 19, 1982

development which have been overlooked by consecutive Liberal and Conservative and Liberal-Conservative governments, which in British Columbia are called Socreds. We would spend $5.4 billion to create 300,000 new jobs. We would spend and we would borrow, but we would do it in such a way that the money was wisely invested so that there would be a return. We would not force people out of work or onto lower wages, as the Liberals and Tories voted for on Friday with Bill C-124. Every Canadian out of work should know that this government's intention is to prolong the recession and force workers to take lower wages, a bottom line Conservative policy.
Two years ago the Department of Finance did a comprehensive evaluation of tax expenditures. Certain kinds of income are given preferential tax treatment. We all know that there were many who earned over $200,000 last year and who paid no income tax at all. These and other loopholes cost Canada $39 billion in 1980 alone. By the end of this tax year the loopholes will have reached $45 billion. Some few of the deductions are fair, such as spousal deductions and deductions for dependent children. Many are not. We in this party believe that the system should be revamped to put cash back into the hands of those who do the work in this country.
Here are just a few of the provisions which should be cut back or eliminated. The fast write-off in resource development; the most recent figures are from 1980, and they cost $1.25 billion. Excess depreciation in the resource sector, $370 million. Fast write-offs in manufacturing, $600 million. Nontaxation of half of capital gains, $800 million in 1980. The $1,000 investment income deduction cost the government $655 million in 1980. The list goes on for pages.
Before the Alsands cancellation the federal government gave the companies $8 million to ensure the project stayed open during negotiations. It was never returned. The government was prepared to give billions of dollars in concession to Alsands to get it under way and guarantee a 20 per cent rate of return.
The alternative energy sector in this country, Mr. Speaker, would replace many of these megaprojects overnight if given the kind of incentives and grants poured into the megas. Surely it is time we broke the stranglehold of the Crown and private hydro and fossil fuel giants. Combinations of tidal, wind, geothermal, solar and biomass can meet in an environmentally and economically sound manner the needs of most of Canada and the world. The global politics of oil and hydro are the chief opposition. The capital strike we witnessed earlier this year in the megaoil projects resulted from a lack of understanding of the energy monopoly by the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). This same minister announced a gift of $2.2 billion to the oil and gas sector to pay them off for this blunder. Those funds are part of this $11 billion borrowing, no doubt.
The minister gave $40 million to Imperial Oil to keep Cold Lake going. Once it died the minister wrote that sum off and with it the taxes hard earned by thousands of Canadians. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has given over $6 million to Hilton hotels in his own riding,
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
contrary to the guidelines of the program. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is responsible for the loss of $125 million to Consolidated Computers, which was recently sold for a paltry $100,000.
In the last four years over $1.5 billion has been shovelled into the nuclear program despite the closure of nuclear facilities in the United States because they are a bad risk and a bad investment. We are producing, at a cost of $100 million a year, heavy water for nuclear reactors when there is no need for it at the heavy water sites in Canada, and no prospects of overseas sales. Perhaps when Argentina drops a nuclear bomb, heaven forbid, on the Falkland Islands, the Liberals will wake up to their folly and their national and international mistakes. These same donkeys will bail out Dome this summer, Mr. Speaker, rather than fund alternatives for a secure Canadian energy future.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, it is clear that no Canadian can accept the borrowing and spending practices of this group across the floor who are wildly out of control. Despite spending over $1 million every working day to advertise their political philosophy at taxpayers' expense, they have come back to this House in less than a month to borrow another $11 billion. In one month that totals $17.6 billion in borrowing authorized by this Parliament and it should be stopped. That is almost $2,000 for every taxpayer in Canada. How many taxpayers have borrowed $2,000 this month, last month or next month at a 20 per cent interest rate? No, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are on the wrong track and should not be supported by this House or the Canadian electorate.
As for the Tories and their intention to filibuster this bill, let them remember the words of their leader: "We have looked for a solution other than the government's, but we could not come up with an alternative. At this moment I do not have a better solution."
Well, Mr. Speaker, the NDP does have a better solution and we do have a better way. Thank you, Mr. Speaker; I will let one of the Neanderthals tell us where they are going to cut.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed to talk about the amendment and this bill, may I say to my friend, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), that I was impressed with his effort to increase the deficit. He talked about a new $2 billion tax cut, $450 million

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
for energy projects, another $2 billion for another government entity called Enterprise Canada, and then somewhere along the line he added another $5.4 billion. He came up to another $10 billion. He said he was going to oppose this bill and suggested, I presume, that the government borrow another $10 billion.
