speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I just hope the hon. member learns how to add. I was proposing what the NDP would do with the $11 billion that the Liberals are proposing to borrow and where we would cut. I hope we can hear from him precisely the same thing.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member is having a difficult time understanding why he is opposing a borrowing bill at the same time as he proposes further massive government expenditures and interference in the economy. It is difficult to be a socialist these days, sir, but he, of course, comes from British Columbia and opposes a government in British Columbia which has at least one decent philosophy which is to not run the province into debt. That province has done exceptionally well in the management of its affairs by keeping down deficits and deliberately controlling its expenditure pattern. This is a pattern that should be followed by this government. If it had done so, the deficit of the federal government this year would be less than $3 billion.
This is the fourth time I have risen in this session of Parliament to speak with respect to borrowing authority legislation. The first bill we received at the opening of this session of Parliament was a bill for $12 billion. That was followed up within not many months with a request for a further $14 billion. The minister said this afternoon that the bill for $6.6 billion, the third borrowing authority bill, received Royal Assent on June 17. We now have before us in the month of July, just four weeks after the last bill received Royal Assent, another bill for an additional $11 billion.
This House has been asked to approve borrowing by this federal government of some $43.6 billion in this one session of Parliament. That is the wealth of 43,600 millionaires expropriated to pay the deficits of this government since it was elected to govern on February 18, 1980. It is unbelievable that Members of Parliament should be asked to allow a government to borrow that kind of money.
It would perhaps be understandable if the minister had shown to us this afternoon when he spoke-and he is not here at the moment; in fact, there is no member of the treasury benches here-where the government could have put that $43.6 billion to use. It could have used it to build Canada, to put people to work, to stimulate the economy of Canada or to make Canada grow. But you and I know, Mr. Speaker, that our country is not growing. Our country is stagnating. Every week thousands more people are laid off from jobs in plants, in the mines, or in the forest industry, with no real hope of being called back.
That is the financial attitude of this government that as of this week has run the net debt of the country to $94 billion and that will, before March 31, 1983, that is before the end of the fiscal year, run that debt up to $107 billion. That is an attitude which cannot be allowed to continue, Mr. Speaker.
The late John George Diefenbaker used to say "Where are we going?" Sir, where are we going as we borrow, borrow and borrow more and more of the wealth and the savings of Canadians and let this crowd handle our money in the ineffectual, improper and impossibly wasteful method that it does?
Canada's debt has become so enormous that it takes one in every three revenue dollars to pay the interest. The interest on the debt is projected this year at $17.7 billion. Let me repeat that fact. One in every three revenue dollars is required to pay the interest.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext: The NDP would like to make that higher.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
The interest alone represents $723 per person per annum. That includes every man, woman, child and babe in arms. Or, expressed in another way, it is $1,864 per taxpayer, for interest alone. The interest represents 4.9 per cent of the gross national product in the country.
This afternoon the hon. member for Skeena talked about further deficits and how spending is stimulative. For a few minutes this afternoon I want to talk about the stimulative effect of debts. I want to say that there is no evidence whatever that government spending, particularly government deficit spending, is in any way stimulative. It may be said that when you spend money at least you put people to work, that people are doing something. But when you spend borrowed money that costs a minimum of 17 per cent for interest-a good part of it now at 19.5 per cent as a result of goofs in the Canada Savings Bond issue last year-you wind up with a situation whereby the dollar borrowed at 17 per cent doubles itself in three and a half years or so, depending upon the compounding. It may take four years to double or it may take less than three and a half years.
We have the situation that if $1 of government money is borrowed and spent allegedly to stimulate the economy, in order just to break even the Government of Canada has to give back $1.50 from taxes in a year and a half. That is not possible. There is not a single government program that can be justified on the basis of the stimulative effect of a deficit, because a deficit is not stimulative. A deficit is, if anything, repressive.
It is the repressive effect of the debt with which the government has saddled Canada that is indeed largely responsible for the economic morass in which we find ourselves. It is no secret that businesses in our country are starved for capital. They are under a liquidity crunch. Businesses cannot support the interest on the debt which they are carrying. When that situation happens, people are not able to replace machinery, people are not able to build, people are not able to create new jobs, because they cannot afford to.
July 19, 1982

1 am involved in some businesses. On a number of occasions 1 have been at board meetings during which we have talked about whether we should make improvements to a business, whether we should buy machinery, certain tooling or perhaps tool up for a new product. When interest rates were down in the 9 per cent and 10 per cent range, we could look with all practicality, to a four-year or five-year payback on investment. Today with interest rates running at a cost to business of somewhere in the range of 20 per cent, you cannot look at a four-year or five-year payback. You have to have the payback within two years because you cannot afford to borrow at that rate unless there is a two-year payback.
This is where we are at because of the massive borrowing that has crowded out the marketplace and has driven up interest rates. We now have a situation where the businesses in our country are suffering from a total lack of liquidity, where investments in new machinery and equipment, unless they can be justified in a two-year payback or less, cannot be made. Research and development cannot be financed unless that research and development can show a payback within two years, because it is not practical to do so.
Yet we have a government which two years back-to-back increased spending by 20 per cent each year. We have a government that is $20 billion in the red. It comes to Parliament for the second time in this fiscal year and says that it wants to borrow money. This time it wants to borrow $11 billion. It just finished borrowing $6.6 billion. We have a government that has no sense of reality as to the cost of money or as to the cost of doing things. It enters into program after program suggesting that the program will stimulate business.
There was a provision in the budget for $3,000 grants to first-time purchasers of houses. It could be used houses. The other day in Scarborough the minister for housing set up an orchestrated presentation of a $3,000 cheque. The man had already purchased a used house, but the minister wanted to give him a $3,000 cheque. When the reporter asked the man whether he needed the $3,000 grant in order to close the deal, he said: "No, I would have bought the house anyway, but it is nice to have the cheque." What did the minister say? He said; "Perhaps he did not need the cheque to buy the house, but he can do some landscaping, purchase some appliances, this, that or the other thing." I point out that that $3,000 grant, for a man who was going to purchase the house anyway, goes into his pocket. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it does not come out of either of our pockets today; it comes out of the pockets of our kids at 19.5 per cent compound interest. What is it for? He might use the money to do some landscaping, to purchase some appliances or perhaps put it in his bank account.
Where was the stimulative effect of that $3,000 of borrowing by the Government of Canada? No new purchase was made, no new commitment was made, no new building was erected. Indeed, it was money paid straight out of the borrowing account to make the minister look good on television. 1 want to say that the minister looked like he usually looks- someone who is not competent to be in any government, let
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
alone this government. Even in this government he is incompetent, which is saying something.
Where are we going? My friends in the New Democratic Party talk about the horrible rip-offs of big business. They do not realize the statistics. Corporate profits in Canada are down from $24 billion to a projected $14 billion, to a projected amount lower than that. Where are we going as company after company is incapable of carrying on and is forced to close its doors, as there are bankruptcies on top of bankruptcies and receiverships on top of receiverships? We have reached the point today where a person has to shop the entire city of Toronto to find anyone who can conceivably act as a receiver because they are all busy. Perhaps a receiver can see him in two, three or four weeks, but he has to get on the waiting list. The only growth industry in the country is the receivership industry. We have a government which comes to Parliament with one program after another, spending money without any thought of constraint, borrowing money and squeezing out the marketplace.
Before referring to the crowding out of the marketplace, 1 remind the House that in early June government representatives attended a conference in Versailles. When they returned from the conference they blamed the United States. They said that the huge American deficit would drive up interest rates and that the government had spent its efforts at Versailles trying to persuade those dastardly Americans that they should not borrow what they were borrowing. I do not think anyone will say that the American debt is not high, but let me point out that the American deficit on a per capita basis is half the amount of our deficit. They tell the Americans that they are wrong, but they do not pay any attention to Canada.
We heard the minister suggest earlier this afternoon that Canadian savings were high and that there was lots of room for savings in Canada, so 1 thought 1 would put on the record of the House a table which was prepared by the Royal Trust company in its booklet entitled "Through A Glass, Darkly: A Medium-Term Canadian Perspective, 1981-86". Actually this table was repeated in a book by Arthur W. Donner entitled "Financing the Future-Canada's Capital Markets in the Eighties". Unfortunately it was written considerably before the present deficit and Mr. Donner was considerably more optimistic when he completed his work in February, 1982, than he would be today. Mr. Donner pointed out in his book that personal savings, as a percentage of the gross national product, of Canadians in 1980 were $14.9 billion. In 1981 he forecast a decrease to $13,148 billion and that since 1982 was to be a recovery year-and we know what kind of a recovery we are having-savings might go up as high as $18 billion.
The government says that it must borrow $17.1 billion in 1982, which is very close to the personal savings of all Canadians in 1982. The government is going to go to the markets of the country to borrow all the new savings of Canadians. We also know that the provinces are in the act. There is not a province during this downturn of our economy which does not have a deficit. Even some western provinces are now having to

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
borrow; even Alberta is borrowing. From where is the money to come?
Until this year the provinces, including the benefits available to them from the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan, had surpluses of borrowing capacity. They could borrow from their pension plans, they had funds available. But in total the provinces will probably be in deficit positions this year and they will have to borrow.
What about business? What about where we build this recovery about which the minister talks? Where will we put the people back to work who the minister says are now being laid off? How do we get the country stimulated and going again? Where are the fresh funds to break the back of this recession-cum-depression? There is not any, not while we have a government which is prepared to soak up, to suck up and to dry up by its grasping hands every bit of savings in the country in order to finance its waste and its spending. This bill must be turned back even when considered on that basis alone. No matter how much we would like the government to spend money, our country cannot afford to go to our markets in the country to borrow money, especially in the amount being demanded by the government.
What have the effects of this borrowing been? We have seen the effects. Since there are not enough savings in this country to satisfy business and government needs here, we have to be a net importer of capital into Canada. Due to the provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act and the attitudes taken in the November 12 budget and the National Energy Program, long-term capital has been driven out of the country. We have had to increase interest rates here so that they are now at least 3 per cent higher than in the United States. I suggest that because of this borrowing requirement there is no hope in the world that interest rates in Canada can drop below that 3 per cent diffrence between here and the United States. Indeed, I suggest that it may well be the fact that as more people in Canada lose confidence in the capacity of this country to grow, develop and become a creative environment, more Canadians and foreigners will remove their money and thereby make the interest differential increasingly higher. This is where this borrowing leads us and this is where the government's spending habits have led us.
Unless an immediate effort is made by Parliament to deal with the crippling deficits which have been imposed by this government and its predecessors, we will not be able to turn our economy around and come out of this recession-cum-depression. We will sink ever lower in the abyss. The future of our children is at stake.
I would like to analyse for a moment what this borrowing authority bill is all about. As you may be aware, Mr. Speaker, if, when borrowing authority is granted to a government, it does not use the borrowing authority, the normal course is that the borrowing authority lapses at the end of the fiscal year. If the borrowing authority is used, permanent debt is then
created. If that debt is paid off in some manner, the government immediately has the right to roll that borrowing authority over again and continue with the same amount of debt.
When we vote for borrowing authority for $11 billion, we are effectively saying to the government that it can on a permanent basis increase the debt of Canada by $11 billion. If bonds are raised under this borrowing authority and those bonds are repaid at some point, the government can then roll the bonds over or issue new bonds to new investors and still stay within the ambit of its total borrowing capacity.
Speaking of borrowing capacity, on July 6 the government had $5.8 billion of unused borrowing authority as a result of its actions this year. It now comes to the House looking for $11 billion. This makes a total borrowing authority of $16.8 billion, nearly $17 billion. So far this year it has used up some $4.5 billion by using hangover borrowing authority from last year, plus a portion of new borrowing authority which was finally granted to it on June 17.
The government has not introduced an acceptable budget. There is every indication that the government will be producing a new budget some time in November of this year. Therefore, why does the government want all this borrowing authority right now? The June 28 budget, which really was not a budget since it did not give proper projections, was indeed a specious piece of paper which indicated that the deficit figures were based on a gross national product dropping only 2 per cent this year. But we all know the projections now are that the gross national product of the country may drop over 8 per cent this year.
The budget was a specious document and will clearly have to be replaced before November 30. On that basis, why do we need more borrowing authority? The fact is that we do not need it. The government already has $5.8 billion in borrowing authority. The fact is that the government has $4.7 billion in the banks. The government has lots of money right now. It has $4.7 billion on deposit in the banks and $5.8 billion in borrowing authority. It has enough right now to pay its bills through to the end of November, and then some. Even with its crazy spending habits and the fact that it is spending $1.4 billion a month more than it receives in taxes, it has enough to carry it through to November. Therefore, why do we need this bill? There is really no need for it at this stage.
What we do need, however, is an inquiry into how government spending takes place. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the House about statements by the former auditor general, Mr. Macdonell, who said last week that what the government must do is analyse its spending program and its priorities. Its spending should be divided into what is absolutely essential, what is desirable and what is non-essential.
Where are we going? There is no effort by this government to priorize its expenditures. Does the government accept the suggestion of our party that there should be a task force of parliamentarians to inquire in detail into the expenditures of the government and the budgetary expenditures of each department in order to determine on a priority basis whether an expenditure is essential, non-essential or just desirable? It does not want that to happen. This should be done.
July 19. 1982

We must review the grant programs of the government and its activities and question whether these programs, while they may be very desirable, are essential. It may be desirable to have expansion in the Canadian broadcasting system, but is it essential? The National Arts Centre is obviously desirable but is it essential? The CHIP program is obviously desirable since it will save home owners money and enable them to get a four or five-year payback, but as 1 said earlier, businesses cannot invest in a four or five-year payback today because money costs too much. Is it essential or just desirable?
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) went over a number of programs which are clearly frills. 1 write to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) almost weekly. When we formed the government, 1 wrote almost weekly to my hon. friend, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), who was the President of the Treasury Board. When 1 received a book from a minister's department, a beautiful brochure or a map, 1 asked "Is it essential? Is it a non-essential frill expense?" My hon. friend, the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), smiles. I think something colourful and beautiful came from her department. There is not a single Member of Parliament who does not get material across his or her desk, is invited to something run by the government, or has been involved in some program, activity or trip. We must ask, are these really essential? Much of it is non-essential puffery. We could reduce expenditures in every department by 5 per cent, certainly administration costs and many others as well, if we considered and determined what is essential and what is non-essential. Sure, some of these expenditures amount only to $60,000, $100,000 or half a million, but they add up enormously.
When one is paying 19.5 per cent to borrow money and when the cost of that borrowed money triples in three and a half years, then the question matters as to whether it is essential, simply desirable, or really non-essential, or is the expense indefensible. Yet the government refuses to appoint a parliamentary committee to inquire into expense based on that logic. Why? It is because it likes it the way it is. It is so accustomed to going around and around the boat, spending and spending, without any real thought as to whose money it is.
The government has the free lunch theory, the theory that if there is a problem, the government should do something. People come into my constituency office and ask, "Is there not a grant or a program for this problem? Can you not help me with it? Can you not get assistance under some government program?" A small telephone booklet came to my office the other day with the names of government programs and grants in it. 1 am sure Your Honour received one. The government subscribes to the free lunch theory that, somewhere along the line the money comes down from the trees, you take it and spend it, you do not have to borrow it and do not have to worry about where it is earned. Well, I never got to this place because someone gave me a free lunch, and I am sure Your Honour did not become a Member of Parliament on the free
Adjournment Motion
lunch theory. Your Honour worked, created and produced. You did not look for a grant. But the money you took out of your pocket with which to pay taxes is being used by this government to further the free lunch theory. But it is not only the money expropriated from people who rake asphalt, drive trucks or work in offices all day, which is being used to pay the government's profligacies. We must also remember that the money the government borrows, and the money which is borrowed and reborrowed, on which we pay 17 per cent to 19.5 per cent interest, multiplies and multiplies. That is a tax which is not on me, because I will never pay it off, and it is not a tax on you, Sir, because you will never pay it off. Is the tax not on our grandchildren? And for what?

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1982-83 MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to speak on Bill C-125, an act to Provide supplementary borrowing authority. The bill is very short, covering only a page and a quarter, but it will be very long in its effects on each and every Canadian. It seeks to obtain authorization for the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to borrow, with the approval of the governor in council, sums of money not exceeding $11 billion, as may be required for public works and general purposes.
The government has projected financial requirements of $17.1 billion this year and some of that requirement will be met through the rundown of Canada's foreign reserves. As I understand it, the government already has something like $10.2 billion in borrowing authority for this year, consisting of $3.6 billion in unused authority from previous years and $6.6 billion from Bill C-111. Therefore, the government has a total borrowing authority of something like $21.2 billion for this year, a figure which is considerably higher than the projected financial requirements of $17.1 billion as outlined in the previous budget.
I think it is also worth noting that in subclause (2) of Clause 2 there is special provision for unused authority of up to $4 billion to be carried over into 1983-84. This leads me to ask where all this money is going, where it is all coming from, and what is happening to Canada and to the Canadian economy.
Over the past 14 years government spending has risen at an unprecedented rate. Using Canada's public accounts as a basis, spending has increased from $12.3 billion in 1968-69, the year the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office, to $78 billion this year, an increase of 534 per cent, yet the population of this nation during this period of time increased from approximately 20 million to 24 million people. A significant portion of this
increase occurred since the re-election of the present government in 1980.
The projected spending of $78 billion this year and a projected deficit of $19.6 billion, which is almost double the projected deficit of last November's budget, has already sent our markets and our dollar into a tailspin, and for good reason. Our gross national debt in March was approximately $135 billion. Interest alone on this debt will cost Canadian taxpayers this year an estimated $17.75 billion.
These numbers are large. They are actually too large for Canadians to grasp in a meaningful way. However, if they are broken down their magnitude becomes more understandable. For example, government spending this year alone at the federal level will be equal to $8,250 per taxpayer. This compares to $1,700 per taxpayer in 1967, the year this Prime Minister took office. To put it another way, federal government spending is now more than six times greater than it was when Mr. Trudeau first came to power and 15 times greater than the amount spent in any of the war years. That is a frightening thought, a frightening amount.
For most of us, a budget is supposed to be a plan which limits expenditures so that they match up with revenue, and expenses should not exceed income. However, that ancient, solidly based philosophy no longer seems acceptable to Ottawa's bureaucrats or politicians.
As I listened to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance and to the apologist today for the finance minister, the hon. member for Charlesbourg (Mr. Bussieres), I could not help but be reminded of the story entitled "Alice in Wonderland". Just imagine the scene in the House of Commons being played by people with different names. First there was Alice. Alice must be the Canadian people who have fallen through the rabbit hole and are watching a band of strange people do very strange things. There was the rabbit that led us down the hole. He is dressed in a very natty suit, wearing a rose in his lapel. He must be the leader. Then there was the finance minister. He must be the white knight who told us in November that four times five was ten and one-half. He has now corrected this to mean $19.6 billion for his budgetary deficit. The present Auditor General, Kenneth Dye, suggests it will really be closer to $22 billion. The Queen of Hearts who stole the tarts must be the energy minister who has stolen the natural resources from the people who developed them. Tweedledum and Tweedledee must be the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien), who supported the Foreign Investment Review Agency and drove out many potential foreign investors that may have established industries in Canada and provided employment for our people.
The cast of the characters is vast. There was the mouse and the duck and the crab and the caterpillar and kings and queens and knaves. I could go on and on, but I know you will remember Mr. Speaker, some of the happenings, such as the Mad Hatter's tea party. You will recall that in the end Alice wakes
July 19, 1982

up and finds that she has been dreaming. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, when this is all over and the Mad Hatter's party is finished, which is when this government falls, that the Canadian people will wake up and realize that it was not a dream, that it was all too true?
In truth, the budget and this borrowing bill have left Canadians feeling somewhat like a burst balloon. Their hopes for the future have evaporated into thin air. Certainly any hope for interest rate relief evaporated when the government announced its deficit projections were wrong by $10 billion.
By the end of this summer, competition for money in Canada's capital markets will most likely drive the prime rate up to 20 per cent or more. In fact, with the federal government going to the money markets for at least $1.5 billion every month for the next 12 months, I predict that interest rates are likely to go through the roof.
Canadians have always believed, at least up until recent months, that this country had a great future. I still believe that Canada and Canadians have a great future. I also know that that future can be realized only if we place a new federal government in Ottawa that adopts new directions and restores confidence to Canadians in their government and in their country.
The secret to our present disastrous and, to use the Prime Minister's own words, crisis economic situation is the complete lack of confidence and trust that Canadians now have in their government. From Atlantic Canada to the tip of British Columbia and then on up to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, the Canadian economy is laid waste. On July 9 it was quite a shock to me to sit in my seat in this House and listen to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) point out that 100 per cent of the population in two towns in his constituency, namely Elsa and Faro, were laid off. Over 600 families in the Yukon are affected. The employment minister's only answer to the hon. member's request was that he was aware of the problem.
Business bankruptcies in Nova Scotia, according to The Chronicle-Herald of Wednesday, July 7, are up by 20 per cent this year over the same period in 1981. What do we find on the national average? In the July 14 Montreal Gazette we read:
Canadian companies forced into bankruptcy in the first half of this year went down owing more than $1 billion-more than double the amount in the corresponding period last year, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said yesterday.
Those are not Tory figures. Those are Liberal government figures, figures provided by the Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
In the first six months, 5,383 Canadian companies went bankrupt, 1,451 more than a year earlier.
Surely we must ask why this is happening. It is because Canadians have been betrayed by the Trudeau administration, betrayed with respect to economic policy, betrayed with respect to energy policies, betrayed with respect to constitutional policy, betrayed with respect to federal-provincial policies and betrayed in our dealings with the outside world.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was referring to him at that time because he was then the leader of the opposition. At that time he outlined his economic program to the electorate in Toronto, stating "We have an economic program for the eighties which will enhance dignity, create opportunities and provide security."
Thirty months later the Canadian people are quite rightly asking, where is that program? The tragedy of the years under the right hon. member for Mount Royal is how we have wasted and are still wasting our potential. I am convinced that Canadians want to see things get better than they are at present and that they could bring this about if they only had a government which would help and not hinder them. The present economic crisis, the chaos, the lack of confidence of Canadians, the frustration, the anger and the despair are not caused by the Canadian people and not by any lack of resources in the second largest land mass in the world, nor by any lack of opportunities but, rather, by a lack of government leadership, by wrongheaded policies, by arrogance, by a lack of knowledge at the top and by the smugness of the people who have been too many years in office.
I have watched this power beget power over the years, but the present situation does not have to be. The answer lies not in our stars, not in Germany or Japan or the United States- the favourite whipping boy of the Prime Minister-but, rather, in this government, a government which has failed Canada miserably.
Our economic problems are not caused by U.S. interest rates. They are not caused by outside forces we cannot overcome. They are caused, if I may say so, by a weak Canadian economy which now provides us with a weak Canadian dollar, all as the result of 14 years of wrong, self-indulgent and politically inspired economic policies. It is people like the Prime Minister, the Turners, the Macdonalds, the Bensons, the Chretiens and the MacEachens who have given us our high interest rates at the 18 per cent to 20 per cent level, our unemployment rate at the 11 per cent level-some 1.3 million people together with another 410,000 additional persons calculated by Statistics Canada to be the number of the hidden unemployed-and our inflation rate year after year, which is now over 11.5 per cent. These men gave us our depression. Our productivity has decreased for four years in a row, and our real wages have been down for four years in a row.
What does the July 12, 1982, editorial in Maclean's have to say under the title "Party or country-which will MacEachen bankrupt first?" It reads:

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
The business community's reaction to Allan MacEachen's budget was swift and vicious: share prices on the Toronto Stock Exchange plummeted 40 points on the morning after, wiping out $2.9 billion in paper profits during the first 60 minutes of trading. Within the same hour ... the Canadian dollar dropped nearly a full cent... These stock market losses came on top of the slide that has cut $66.25 billion out of stock prices in the past year.
Over the years I can well remember the Liberals saying at election time: "Tory times are hard times; vote Liberal." In retrospect, as I look back over ten federal elections and some 25 years I must agree that when my party was in power Tory times were difficult times. They were difficult because we had to deal with the economic wreckage the Grits left behind them. However, in their lust for power, the Liberals, along with their New Democratic pallies, defeated the minority Conservative government and found themselves back in power after making misleading promises about lowering gasoline costs. This time the Liberals have to try to clean up their own mess. Grit times today are grim times for everyone to see and all to experience, and it is a situation which will not be forgotten too soon by all Canadians.
In considering the issues, we all know that Canada's economy is influenced greatly by the outside world and that much of the outside world is also facing economic difficulties. But clearly our lack of leadership, direction and policy on the part of the party in power has seriously worsened our economic situation.
What about our inflation? In my opinion our inflation has been caused in large measure by a complete lack of government restraint in spending and in revenue-collecting since 1972-73, resulting in government debts, which total in excess of $77 billion over the ten years ending in 1981-82. The deficit for this year is predicted at close to $20 billion, while Maclean's, as I said a moment ago, says it will reach at least $22 billion in the fiscal year beginning April 1. All through these years the fiscal policy of the government has ignored the monetary policy of the government and the Bank of Canada, so that the tight monetary policy has not succeeded in containing inflation. Every year there has been ever-increasing borrowing by the government, competing for funds with the private sector, and in 1982-83 government spending on a national accounts basis will increase by an estimated 22 per cent over last year. The second largest spending envelope of the federal government is now in the payment of interest on our debt charges, which the government says will cost some $17.7 billion this financial year. One tax dollar out of every four is now used to service the government's debt, compared with one tax dollar out of every nine only eight years ago.
The government cannot say that it was not warned about this economic catastrophe. When I served as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee the new auditor general at that time, Mr. James Macdonell, stated in his 1974-75 report that the government was losing, or was close to losing, control over the public purse. That is strong language from any auditor general, but coming from its own auditor general, the government should have altered the course of its ship of state before it landed on the rocks of fear, despondency and economic collapse. However, unfortunately no one on the opposite side
was listening. No one wanted to listen, and now that the ship is foundering, all the government can do is to look for scapegoats and try to lay the blame everywhere but the one place where it rightfully belongs. I say to hon. members opposite that if the government is serious about battling inflation, the government must give the public an example and must restrain and discipline itself if it wishes the people to restrain and discipline themselves. But this government to date has only carried out what I call cosmetic changes, and it is not fooling anyone.
How can hon. members opposite say that they are practising restraint when the "one billion" white elephant, Mirabel, continues to lose money at the rate of approximately $1 million a week? How can hon. members opposite justify their claims to restraint when they are purchasing new Challenger jet aircraft at a cost of $27 million? They cannot even find the funds to rebuild the fishermen's wharf at Riverport, Nova Scotia destroyed some two years ago and help re-establish a viable fishing industry at that port. How can hon. members opposite say they are practising restraint when they spend yearly some $225 million on their own public information and advertising budget, not to tell the people what they are doing but to try to hide from the public what is happening in Canada? Hon. members opposite spent $300,000 for a lively bash on the day the Post Office became a Crown corporation and spend $500,000 each year to give new briefcases to the public servants of Canada. They then have the gall to tell this House they are practising restraint! I say to all hon. members opposite that they do not even know the meaning of the word.
In the patronage area of spending, on government services alone spending increased from $4 billion in 1980-81 to $4.7 billion in 1981-82, an increase of 17 per cent in government patronage for lawyers and other fees. Where were the 6 per cent guidelines then? Where were the 6 per cent guidelines hon. members opposite now impose on some 1.2 million senior citizens who are singled out to pay for the mistakes of the government?
To complete the destruction of the Canadian economy, this administration, without any authorization from the Canadian electorate, instituted a constitutional war with the provinces which occupied most of 1980 and 1981. Hon. members opposite destroyed confidence. They failed to reach oil and gas agreements quickly with the producing provinces. They caused delays so that we have lost the Alsands tar sands plant and the Cold Lake project. They caused delays in the development of the Hibernia oil field off the coast of Atlantic Canada because of their determination to control and manage these resources. Then the Right Hon. Prime Minister ended all that with a declaration of war on the provinces by saying that co-operative federalism no longer exists. On January 12, 1982, the Right Hon. Prime Minister confirmed this declaration of war on the provinces by ending any attempt whatsoever at co-operation through the former DREE department. We now have DRIE instead of DREE with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) at its head. There is a megaprojects coordinator for each province, although there are no signs-
July 19, 1982

certainly not in my province-of any megaprojects to coordinate.
The damage of all this to our economy is obvious. There can be no confidence or trust upon which an expanding economy can be based when the federal government is entangled and engaged in such destructive, vicious, uncaring, unheeding and arrogant policies.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) brought in the budget on November 12, 1981 he said that it had three themes: restraint, equity and economic renewal. On each of these grounds his budget was a complete failure. On September 9, 1980, speaking in Halifax, the capital of my province, he said it was in order to create jobs, improve living standards and promote greater equity that he took on the position of minister of finance. In light of what has happened since that time, I ask in all fairness how he can continue to hold on to that position!
We are sometimes asked about alternative policies. Every once in a while we read in the media that the Conservative Party has no alternative policies. Certainly we have no alternative policies like those proposed by the leader of the NDP who suggests that a magic wand be waved so that interest rates in Canada be reduced by 5 to 10 per cent. We know that such a step would mean wage and price controls, exchange controls and total state control of every aspect of our lives. The answer, of course, is not that simple. What is needed is more long-term changes. 1 can assure the House that within six months of taking office, my party would start the Canadian economy well back on the road to growth and prosperity. We did it in 1957 and in 1958, and we can do it again.

speechtext:
We got the economy rolling in 1957 and 1958, and we can do it again. Our alternative policies and thrusts can be seen in the budget of December 11, 1979. These thrusts are still basically right for Canada. 1 believe that we could, upon taking office-with a majority from the Canadian people- restore confidence to ordinary Canadians in the private sector by throwing out this rehashed budget introduced by the Liberals.
We would end tax harassment and government legislative discouragement to risk takers, the people who are so badly needed in our economy at the present time. A new budget
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
would be brought in within a reasonable period of time to settle the ground rules and outline and establish the framework for a two or three-year period, providing the stability that the business world needs for expansion and restoring the Canadian economy.
We would bring about changes in the present National Energy Program, and reduce the present discrimination against the foreign and the Canadian entrepreneur. A reduction in the tax burden on industry is also required to encourage Canadian exploration and development.
As a Nova Scotian, I personally believe that in Canada we have to utilize our maritime position, our Arctic resources and our tremendous coasts, lakes and rich continental shelf. We have to develop our own shipping fleet and focus attention upon our fishing industry. Our main objective should be the utilization and development of our resources on, in and under the waters that surround our vast shores. For all too long this government has engaged in navel gazing. Perhaps that is why the country is presently going belly up.
In my opinion, this government, as is usual with Liberal governments, confines its gaze to the bulging population residing in central Canada while the extremities of the country, especially the coastal regions, are neglected. I believe that the coastal shipbuilding industry, especially the east coast industry, with the discovery of massive offshore oil reserves, has fantastic potential. Billions of dollars will have to be spent on new vessels in order to develop the offshore resources in the next ten years. However, shipbuilding is a most unnatural industry, one that requires the most support of the central government if it is to be effective and successful. In most shipbuilding nations government provides shipbuilders with generous subsidies, tax breaks and investment allowances, but Canada does not provide any of these. In order to develop the industry in this international, cutthroat market, nations must have well developed shipbuilding policies and dependable financial arrangements for the benefit of workers and owners as well as builders. Canada has no such policy. Shipbuilding in Canada is an industry which has important local as well as regional implications, but unfortunately the government has failed to catch the vision of the opportunities the industry could offer the nation. With federal policymakers preoccupied with troubles at the nation's centre, it appears that we will be passing up another fantastic opportunity on our east coast. That lost opportunity could take with it the dream of the Canadian merchant marine. Three times in our history the Canadian nation has developed a sizeable merchant marine, and each time federal indifference has wrecked that fleet.
It is this indifference to Atlantic Canada's needs that is the real core of some of our problems. We need policies that would strengthen the various local industries. Just sending money into an area for what I call cosmetic, make work projects, is not the answer. For example, the federal and provincial governments have spent millions of dollars to keep the Cape

July 19, 1982
Supplementary Borrowing Authority
Breton steel industry alive. A long-term, positive shipbuilding program could be the catalyst that would set the industry on the road to recovery.
It is estimated that three million tonnes of steel will be needed to manufacture ships for Canadian needs within the next decade. All that is needed to bring this type of development about is a national policy and a national will to carry it out. Without a national long-term policy and direction, companies will not make the investment that is required for development.
It would take investments of $20 million to $100 million per year to keep present Canadian yards competitive with new technologically advanced yards in other nations. Our competition is receiving tremendous help from subsidies. British ship builders, for example, receive 30 per cent, the French receive about 25 per cent, while we in Canada receive about 9 per cent. As a matter of fact, foreign buyers are given a better break when buying Canadian made ships than Canadians are. The government will provide financing at 8.75 per cent for a foreign buyer, but a Canadian buyer who wants to build a ship must go to a bank and pay interest rates as high as 20 per cent or more.
Canada is the only nation in the world with a shipbuilding potential of any consequence which does not have a program to assist its nationals to finance the acquisition of ships locally.
As Conservatives, when we form the next government-and that will be as soon as the next election is called-we intend to change this policy and stimulate our shipbuilding industry for the benefit of offshore use as well as for the benefit of the fishing industry. As Conservatives, we will once again welcome foreign investment.
1 cannot help but wonder about this government's concern about foreign investment, Mr. Speaker. 1 would invite any member of the government to come to Nova Scotia, to Bridgewater, which is just 12 miles from my home town of Lunenburg. They should visit the Michelin plant there, which is the result of French investment. Anyone who remembers the town before Michelin and sees it as it is today will realize the tremendous benefit of foreign investment in the Canadian economy. In my opinion, our need for capital will be immense for the rest of the twentieth century. That need simply cannot be met without foreign investment and foreign loans.
We would make our preference for private-sector ownership and management of the economic system very clear, with policies devised to give room to take risks, to innovate and to grow. The operations of Crown corporations would be reviewed and reduced so long as the private sector could fill any gap that might occur. I believe it is well past the time for a thorough and proper review of our economic future and our relations with our best friend and customer, the United States. The problems that relate, for example, to the boundary issues alone between our two countries, as well as fishing agreements-have been allowed to drift, Sir, for far too long. What may very well have been resolved at the political level now seems destined to end up in continued disputes and bitter controversy between our two countries, which can only be harmful to our own development. I am convinced that within a
very short period of time we could turn around the Canadian economy dramatically and restore it by restoring confidence and trust in ourselves, our government and our nation. It can, Sir, and must be done.
Obviously there are just two clear choices for Canada. The Conservative Party believes in a federal Canada, a federal state with 11 strong governments. It believes in the private sector. We believe in private initiative and private ownership of the economy. We believe in a mixed-market economy, and in the fact that none of us will retain any human or personal rights unless we have a largely privately-owned economic sector. We believe in co-operative federalism and the partnership of our five great regions.
The alternative is the Liberal-NDP alliance, which obviously does not believe in a federation for Canada, an alliance which is anti-province and which is for a centralized, Unitarian government for Canada. It is an alliance which ignores our vast land, our varying regions, and the need for unity and diversity. The alliance is anti-private sector and anti-private ownership and initiative, and against the right to ownership of private property.
Both of these parties, for example, voted against our proposal that the right to ownership of property be included in the Charter of Human Rights, just as it was in the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights, and as it is in other countries. Life, liberty and the right to property was our proposal, but the Liberal-NDP alliance voted together to remove the guaranteed right to ownership of property in this land. Let us never forget what that alliance brought out in the Charter of Rights.
The Liberal-NDP alliance is calling for the centralization of all political and economic power here in Ottawa. It is pro government ownership and control. It is pro granting of enormous supervisory and regulatory power to the bureaucrat, who becomes not dependent on the people of Canada but, rather, on our master, who takes the fruit of the worker's labour while fashioning more burdens for the workers to carry.
1 cannot support that type of government, and I hope the Canadian electorate will recognize what they are voting for when they next go to the polls.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that we must build a Canada where people respect the land, a Canada where people respect the sea and the environment, where we do not squander and abuse our good fortune; a Canada where we respect the law and the rights of others; a Canada where people respect and reward initiative, where excellence is encouraged, and where the work of every individual is recognized. That is the type of Canada that I wish to see, and that is why I support the amendment moved today by the Right Hon. Leader of the Conservative Party (Mr. Clark).

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on this bill today. It gives me an opportunity to talk about some of the myths created as a result

If hon. members cannot believe that from the so-called socialist government, let us have a look at the American government. Revenues for April and May in the United States indicate that this year's budget, the one which finishes in the fall of 1982, will be in deficit by $124 billion. Why? Because the revenues have fallen off significantly in the months of April and May due to the world recession. That recession was not caused by this government, it was a worldwide recession principally caused by the Reagan economic policy in the United States.

Mr. Speaker, the point 1 was trying to make is that the increased government deficit is not, in a major way,
caused by increases in spending. The actual facts are that 79 per cent of all increase in the deficit is caused by decreases in revenue brought about by world recession. Other governments, such as the American government, are finding exactly the same thing happening. Between the two budgets only one dollar in five of the increase in the deficit was caused by an increase in government spending. Half of that was caused by spending which did not happen in the last year, and the other half was mostly caused by additional spending because of the recession.
The Canadian public is not aware of the essential point. It has not been made aware of it by the media; confusion has been sown by the opposition. The essential point is simply that four dollars out of every five of the increased deficit was caused by a decrease in revenue, a decrease in revenue caused by a world recession. That is a fundamental point for Canadians to understand what has happened. Government spending has not gone wild. It is the simple fact that we are in a world recession and revenues have fallen. I will demonstrate later how that has happened in the United States as well as in Canada.
The second myth is the notion that all government spending is in the same order. Let me look at that. There are two basic kinds of spending. The first one is what we call transfers, that is, transfers from the federal government to other governments in terms of health, welfare and so on. I am referring to these kinds of transfers to provinces and to municipalities. There are transfers to people in terms of old age pensions, various forms of pensions, children's allowance or family allowances. There are transfers to corporations in the form of subsidies. There are transfers to funds like the Western Development Fund. There is a whole series of transfers. Also there are transfers to people who own Canada savings bonds, from whom the government borrows money. These are transfers from one Canadian to another. Only about 1 per cent is actually transferred out of the country.
These transfers represent 78 per cent of all federal government spending. Another 2 per cent is in capital spending; in other words, when one acquires capital and builds buildings. Only 20 per cent is in operating the government, such as running the Post Office, the Department of National Defence and all other areas of government. The costs of transferring that money are all in that 20 per cent. When we talk about governments taking from the people, we are talking about the area of goods and services or 20 per cent of the spending which runs all government departments such as the Department of National Defence. That 20 per cent buys our planes and does many things.
If we are really looking at things in a thoughtful way and trying to find what are the answers, rather than making noises, making fun of the government, destroying the government or defeating the government, then we must look at these transfers in an intelligent way. How large is the $20 billion in terms of the gross national product? If I say that 1 spend $20,000 a

year, it does not indicate anything about what that does to me. For example, if I make $40,000 per year and I spend $20,000, I am doing very well. If I make $10,000 per year and I spend $20,000, than I am doing very badly. It is the same with a country. The gross national product of this country for next year will be around $359 billion. That is the gross national product. The value of all goods and services, everything done in the country, will be $359 billion.
The Government of Canada, in terms of goods and services, is taking $20 billion out of that $359 billion. The other $70 billion which the government will spend in 1982-83, the year about which we are talking, the year which the borrowing is for, is transferred from one Canadian to another. It is not taken out of the economy.
How does this compare in terms of the amount spent on goods and services as a percentage of the gross national product? It is about 5.2 per cent of the gross national product. Until approximately 1953 that was about 10 per cent of the gross national product. The amount the government spent on goods and services was about 10 per cent of the gross national product. Then it started to decline, and it declined until about 1965 when it became 6 per cent of the gross national product. Since 1965 it has stayed around that level. It is 5.2 per cent, which is not a very large portion of the gross national product.
1 remind hon. members that the other $70 billion that the government will spend in 1982-83 will be transferred from one Canadian to another. It may be suggested that we are transferring money from the wrong Canadian to the wrong Canadian. 1 believe that the question of who gets the transfers is what we should be considering, and not ascribing this entire amount to government spending. If one were to listen to the opposition, one would think that the Government of Canada is taking 25 per cent of everything away from Canadians. That is not the case. The government is taking 5.2 per cent of the gross national product from Canadians. While it takes a lot more than the 5.2 per cent, it is transferred back. All but 5.2 per cent is transferred back, and I think it is very important for Canadians to understand this.
Another myth is that we are in debt such as we have never been before. This myth arises from a terrible distortion, that is, that this borrowing bill, is creating a debt situation which has never been seen before by Canadians. The net national debt, which will be approximately $200 billion or $300 billion by next year, is approximately 30 per cent or less of the gross national product. While this sounds like a large amount of money it should be compared to that in previous years. In 1926-27 the national debt was 45 per cent. In the middle of the depression it went up to 66 per cent. At the end of the war it was 109 per cent of the gross national product. In the 1950s it was in the range of 30 per cent to 35 per cent. Now, in 198283, it is at 30 per cent.
Is that something that Canadians cannot live with? Canadians are being told by the opposition, principally the Tories, as well as the media, that we are in a doomsday situation and that we cannot handle this kind of debt. However, 80 per cent

1 receive many letters these days from what I suspect is a group which travels around the country writing up these letters because they all seem to be the same. Let us review the situation in the United States to see if there are any comparisons between the problems we are facing and the problems facing the American government under so-called Reaganomics. These figures are difficult to compare because our fiscal year begins on April 1 and ends on March 31, whereas the American government's fiscal year begins on October 1 and ends on September 30. However, it appears that our deficit in 1982-83 will be approximately $19.6 billion; the United States deficit will be somewhere between $150 billion and $160 billion. The revenues are falling and falling in the United States. According to this article, their deficits for this year ending in September will be somewhere between $125 billion and $150 billion. Next year's deficit will certainly be in the order of $150 or $170 billion.

Let us get back to the excessive government spending and mismanagement of this great country of ours. The first thing was the National Energy Program. It too was alluded to by the previous speaker. with energy self-sufficiency regardless of cost. We would not be dependent on the unstable supply of foreign oil.

say:

Obviously the people across the aisle have never read "The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire" to see what happened back in those times. During the period when the Reagan government and Congress in the United States cut taxes and cut government spending, this mob across the aisle keeps raising taxes and

adding to a staggering national debt through deficit spending policies. Now it wants to borrow $11 billion more.
The Fraser Institute in Vancouver has published some very interesting Canadian statistics, Mr. Speaker. The institute's tax index shows that the tax bill of the average family has increased by 515 per cent since 1961. Bonds which the federal government issued to cover deficits are essentially deferred taxation-we all know that-since tax revenue must ultimately be raised to pay the carrying charges and redeem the principal. There are 24.5 million of us, of whom 20 million are able to speak English, 7.4 million are able to speak French.

Again, the moral: Bilingualism and keeping Quebec in Canada costs a lot of money.

We all know that the situation in our country is worse now than in any country in the industrialized world.

We rank lowest in the industrialized world. I have here the figures on the industrial production rate and I just found out that last year Canada declined 10.5 per cent. That is the worst performance in the industrialized world. Next after us is the United States where the economy went down 8 per cent. Australia is third, down 5 per cent. The other countries have a better record than Canada and the United States. It is the same story on the stock market. If you follow the price of shares here in Canada, you will note a similar trend. The price of shares in Canada dropped by some 41 per cent between 1981 and 1982, against only 16 per cent in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, it is patently clear that the economy in Canada is in a worse shape than in other countries and the Canadian problem now needs a Canadian solution. We cannot blame the world situation for our economic woes, because the federal and provincial governments must share the blame as well.

I think we are going to have to wake up in this country and start developing and planning a national investment policy. As I said, we do not have it. The goal should be to increase our wealth as a nation, to increase our ability to provide services to the people, and to increase our net worth as a nation. I think we can do that. We have the people and the resources. If we do not have some imagination, leadership and planning-and perhaps those are democratic socialist ideas but we certainly do not have them today-our nation will not thrive in the years that lie ahead.
I should like to point to three countries which have done well after virtually being destroyed during the Second World War. I am referring to Japan, France and Germany. I point to those three economies to remind the House how well they have done and how well they are doing. Also 1 remind the House where they were some 30 or 35 years ago. 1 notice that one of the first things they did after the Second World War was to decide to rebuild their economies, economies they would own as Frenchmen, Germans or Japanese. It was not a question in any of those countries of whether or not they would build a German, French or Japanese car. They would not even ask that question. They built those cars, but we in Canada do not have a Canadian car. It is not a question in those countries now of whether or not they are getting into high technology or advanced technology. They are just doing it in those countries. For example, in Japan they have five times the population, but they have 40 times the young people in electrical engineering schools that we have in Canada.
Last year as a nation, in terms of research and development, we invested one hundred and some odd million dollars, whereas the Japanese put in over $2 billion. They go out and do those things. In some countries they have democratic socialist governments. In other countries like Japan they do not have a democratic socialist government, but they have planning and they have a policy to own and control their own economies so that they, as Japanese, as French or as Germans, can make their own decisions.
I maintain that our failure to do that as a country is the biggest reason we are in such serious trouble now. We have the consequences of that coming home each and every single day as we see lay-offs in the manufacturing industry and lay-offs in the resource industry from one part of Canada to the other.
Back in 1608 it was Cartier who was really one of the founders of Canada. At that time the country was being built on the premise of exporting beaver pelts and the pelts of other animals to Europe and of importing finished or manufactured goods. I suppose we still have that old philosophy in Canada

where we try constantly to export raw materials, whether they are natural gas, oil or forest products, and import finished goods.
Let me take a look at the consequences of that policy. In 1970 we had a trade deficit in manufacturing of $2.5 billion. In 1981 our trade deficit was up to $21 billion or $22 billion in manufactured goods. In 1969 we had 6 per cent of world trade. In 1979 we were down to 4 per cent of world trade. I expect now that it is approximately 3 per cent. The Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) rises every month and talks about how happy he is to have a trade balance in the country. We have a trade balance in the country, but I think we are one of the only countries, if not the only country in the world, which has a trade balance and a deficit in our balance of payments. Our deficit in the balance of payments last year was some $9.1 billion. The reason for that deficit is that we have interest flowing out to outside or foreign investors. We have dividends which are flowing out, and we have the consequences of a branch plant economy. We have the wealth and resources with which we could be producing in Canada. These products could be owned by Canadians and purchased by the United States. Just because we have a lower dollar does not always mean that the branch plant of a foreign-based multinational will produce in Canada. What they will often do is produce in the United States or Japan and import that good or product into Canada.
I believe very strongly that we will have to restructure the economy so that we as Canadians own it. When we go on the money markets to borrow money, we should borrow it as loan capital, not equity capital, so that when we pay off the loan we own the house, the mine, the store or whatever we borrowed the money for as Canadians.

In conclusion 1 want to suggest positively three or four areas in which we should be spending the money that we have in the country, provincially and federally, and where we should be putting some of our savings.
The first area I want to mention is the entire area of advanced technology and high technology. Just recently the Science Council of Canada issued a report entitled, "Planning Now for an Information Society". In the report we were warned that we are now in a new era and that if we do not move very quickly, we will lose an awful lot of what we have and end up importing more and more of the advanced technological devices and parts in the world of tomorrow. It indicated among other things that advanced technology is moving so fast that we are being left behind. For example, it indicated that the power of computers has increased 10,000 times in the past

15 years, while the price of each unit of performance has decreased by 100,000 times in the last 15 years. Also it indicated that in 1990 we will be producing pocket calculators with more power than today's most powerful computers. This is how fast we are moving in the area of advanced technology. My suggestion is that we should be doing like the Japanese, the French, the British or the Americans. We should be putting some more money and funding into advanced technology. We should be producing these goods, services and products right here in Canada.
We can do this in many ways. The Conservative Party does not believe in putting any money into this because they want the multinationals to make all the decisions; they will put their money into the United States, Japan or elsewhere. It is about time that we took the lead as a nation and started investing some of our funds in this sector. Of all industrial states we have less public involvement in the new technology. I suggest that we will have to move in this area.
There are four areas in which I think we should specialize. We should be applying advanced technology to produce the machinery necessary for specialization and to enable us to become very good in four areas. I think two of them are naturals because of our geography. One is communications and the other is transportation. In communications we are already fairly good. We have developed things like Telidon. We are very good at satellite communications. We are very good in my province at fibre-optics. We have a little plant in Saskatoon called Sed Systems, Inc. which was part of the Canadarm. We have Spar Aerospace in Toronto and Montreal. We have many companies, some publicly owned and some privately owned, which are very good in communications. Because of our geography, we must continue to specialize and to provide goods in our markets so that we can export aggressively in the world in the area of communications.
The second area which is a natural is transportation. Again it is because of our geography. 1 do not understand why we as Canadians are not as good at putting trains on the tracks as are the Japanese, the French or the British. We still have transcontinental trains which run along, like the good old days, at about 18 or 19 miles per hour. One can almost pass them on horseback. That is not good enough. 1 think as Canadians we will have to specialize in transportation.
Another area is food and agriculture. We are a great producer of food in this country. We have a tremendously productive agricultural sector. I think we will have to start putting more funding into that area to help feed some of the poor people of the world. We should export our farm machinery technology to the developing world to ensure that Asians, Africans, South Americans and others can produce their own food and eventually become self-sufficient. We should continue doing research into the field of food production, agriculture and forestry. We should take the lead in these areas. We should be involved in biotechnology, for example; not the Japanese, not the French, not the British or the Germans. That is the third area.

The last area 1 would mention is resources. Our country has tremendous resources. One of our problems is that we have tended to export those resources in their raw and unrefined state throughout the world. These resources are finite and they will eventually run out. We are now running out of much of our conventional oil. It is time that we began to process more of those resources at home. Since we have resources such as hydroelectricity, it is time that we started to manufacture machinery to mine and process those resources in Canada. When I look at other countries of the world 1 find that we are producing very little machinery in this country. There are very few companies which manufacture these machines. In 1980 our deficit in machinery trade was $5.7 billion. 1 suspect that that figure is significantly higher in 1982. We are producing less machinery all the time.
1 recently spoke to an industry spokesman who told me that in the area of computers alone our deficit by 1990 will be approximately $10 billion.
1 suggest that when Canada borrows money for investment we should specialize in four or five areas. These areas include transportation and communication, agriculture and resources and the new high and advanced technologies. If we were to do this through a national plan along with co-operative federalism with the provinces and the federal government working together, instead of the jigsaw network of programs which exist today-a LEAP program here, a LIP program there-we could become very successful. Instead of the government squandering hundreds of millions of dollars, which perhaps only temporarily raises the hopes of some people that it will give them temporary jobs, part of that money should be put into four or five areas where the government could specialize and supply our own domestic market. This would put people to work, and develop industries on a large and competitive scale to enable us to export to the international market.
We have the resources and the education. The Japanese are capable of doing this on a small island with no resources at all. If they can do it, we can do it as well, if not even better. For example, the Japanese recently decided to specialize in pollution control equipment and export that technology to other parts of the world. 1 am sure they will be very successful. We just do not have the leadership which can make decisions like that in this country.
I reiterate that we need a fundamental change and the restructuring of the economy in this country so that we will have Canadian ownership, Canadian industry and Canadian investment. In this way we will be able to own our own homes and businesses.
My concluding point is that if the government wants to put people to work it should be putting our money into the housing industry, rather than helping multinational oil companies as the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) did. As the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) says so often, the housing industry is an all Canadian industry. We build houses for Canadians, we use Canadian parts and
components and we put forestry workers back to work. Many of the furnishings, such as iron and steel used in constructing houses, are also produced in Canada. This is one short-term policy which could be developed by the government. As well, the government can continue its aid to farmers who are competitive, productive and support a large segment of our nation. With that, I urge the House to think positive and bring forth new and fresh ideas and to stop some of the b.s. type of rhetoric which we heard from the hon. member for Simcoe South which is a disgrace not just to members but to any intelligent Canadian.
