subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-USE OF SUBLIMINAL MESSAGES ON ROCK MUSIC RECORDINGS
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-USE OF SUBLIMINAL MESSAGES ON ROCK MUSIC RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 9 of this year 1, along with my colleague, the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang), asked questions of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) dealing with product labelling as it applies to the recording industry and some of the rock music which that industry produces and distributes. The matter pertained to what we could call subliminal, hidden lyrics or messages on certain rock music recordings.
Following that question and answer from the minister, 1 received a further answer from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs informing me that this matter comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Communications, hence the matter being raised tonight.
While the technique of recording hidden messages or lyrics on some rock music has been going on for some time-I believe it was in the sixties that it first came to light involving the much popular recording artists The Beatles-it has again surfaced, causing a great deal of concern among many of our citizens, both young and old alike.
The most recent issue of this concern came to my attention from a number of my constituents following a public affairs program on a local London station on this subject. During that program it was shown how the use of subliminal influence techniques are used by some popular rock music groups. Following this radio broadcast, the issue received considerable attention-I believe the radio station received something like 400 calls immediately following that program-and much attention was focused on this subject in high school, church groups and other community groups interested in this subject. It seems to be a fundamental concern on the part of many that the public should be made aware of the existence of these largely unnoticeable, perception-effecting techniques.
In the Oxford dictionary, subliminal is defined as "below the threshold of sensation or consciousness ... so as to influence opinion or behaviour without being consciously perceived." A subliminal message is a message that is below a discernible level. For example, your conscious mind hears one thing, but your subconscious mind can pick up the other. Some people feel that subliminal persuasion is as close to mind control as you can get.
I am sure hon. members remember just a few years ago when a great deal of concern centred on subliminal advertising suspected of being used on television and in movie theatres. To my understanding, because of public concern expressed at that time, that type of advertising is no longer used.

July 19, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Since this matter was raised, 1 have been overwhelmed by the interest shown in it, and the support 1 have received from across the country, even from the United States. As a matter of fact, this same issue was raised on the floor of the United States Congress just two weeks ago. The concern being expressed is not a concern in favour of censorship or the imposition of morality. We cannot do that. We can, however, restrict immorality. This is the issue, especially when some of these suspected subliminal messages contain messages which society today, for the most part, would term to be immoral. There is a feeling on the part of many people who have communicated with me that the public should not be subjected to hidden messages of any kind, immoral or moral, for it can be argued that the subliminal technique could be used to promote what many would term to be good influencing messages as well as messages which might be harmful.
An issue such as this generates an emotional response. As well as receiving an enormous amount of support, 1 have been criticized for raising this issue, especially when we have so many other problems with which to deal today. I want to say for the record that I have not spent all my time on this subject, as anyone who reads Hansard will attest. But as responsible Members of Parliament 1 feel we must concern ourselves with many different issues raised and brought to our attention by our constituents.
1 suppose the bottom line in this matter is to ask the recording industry at least to investigate and co-operate, and either to label such suspected recordings or, better still, to refrain from producing and distributing such material.
According to my investigation, at least, much of this recorded material has been produced outside this country in the United States and in Europe, mainly in England, so perhaps we have to look at the distribution methods on the part of the recording industry in this area.
When we think of the many problems facing us today, we must remember that a nation is only as good as its people. I would sooner be on the side of those who influence for good than on the side suspected of having a harmful influence on our society. I would welcome a further response to this matter from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-USE OF SUBLIMINAL MESSAGES ON ROCK MUSIC RECORDINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) and the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) have indeed touched upon what 1 too feel is an important point.
1 would just like to explain again that since the arts and cultural branch of the Department of the Secretary of State was transferred in 1980, cultural policy concerns pertaining to Canadian cultural industries, including the sound recording industry, have been the responsibility of the Department of Communications. At present the Canadian sound recording industry is undergoing an extensive examination to determine what support, if any, is required to help it meet its needs and
opportunities. As hon. members are no doubt aware, this industry represents one of the most important cultural activities in Canada, since it provides society with most of the access to the music we enjoy and use in our daily lives.
As the hon. member pointed out, many years ago, during the 1960s, a limited number of foreign producers used the process of backward masking as a new gimmick to attract media attention to records in the marketplace. A few prominent recording artists such as Led Zeppelin and the Beatles did experiment with this technique whereby a record, if played in reverse, would play back different music or lyrics. The fad quickly died down then but, admittedly, has resurfaced lately.
It is supposed by some that the original motivation was strictly to attract attention to the album and not to influence the listeners subiiminally. Experts from both the scientific community and the record industry, including the late Marshall McLuhan, have studied this subject and have stated that since the messages are directly audible, well publicized and not imprintable in the mind unless the listener does reverse the record, it is not a form of subliminal persuasion. However, I will say that the concerns of the hon. members are valid in principle should this practice be used by the industry to the extent where record production would subiiminally influence the listener's mind.
In this regard, the Department of Communications has passed on these concerns to the Canadian record industry associations and will maintain an interest in following this subject should anything new arise.
I would like to add, finally, that the occurrences of this practice are extremely negligible, considering the tens of thousands of records that are produced each year. Also, it is unfortunate that the recording industry tends to suffer mostly from negative publicity such as this when it contributes so much to our fabric of life. I was heartened to see in a recent issue of Maclean's magazine an article which reported on the great success our young Canadian recording talent is having in the global marketplace. In fact, this year, the best year in our history, Canadian artists have outperformed every other country in the world in an otherwise down-sided global economy, and these ambassadors of Canadian culture deserve our utmost support.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-TAX ON FUEL USED IN FOOD PRODUCTION
AGRICULTURE-TAX ON FUEL USED IN FOOD PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been said many times in this House and in the country that the country is suffering a crisis in confidence. 1 believe the crisis stems in large part from a lack of confidence in the government. Canadians realize every passing day that the government has failed to fulfil many of the promises and commitments it made during the course of the election campaign in the deep winter of 1980.
1 raised one of these questions in question period last Friday when I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to
July 19, 1982

explain to the House what happened to the special price structure he had advocated in the community of Alvinston, Ontario, on January 31, 1980, when he said that fuels used in the course of farm production would be exempt from federal tax. We know that commitment was not fulfilled. What is more shocking is that the minister stated that the energy program is supported by all members of the Liberal Party, including himself.
The minister is clearly on record as supporting the price structure for farm fuels in Canada. That means he supports the fact that 60 cents out of the price of every gallon of fuel the farmer burns goes to the federal government coffers in the form of tax. I think it is worth putting on the record what comprises that 60 cents. There is a corporate tax of 10 per cent or six cents per gallon; the petroleum compensation charge of 18 cents per gallon; the Canadian ownership charge of four cents per gallon; the petroleum gas revenue tax of seven cents per gallon; the incremental oil revenue tax of five cents per gallon; a 9 per cent federal sales tax or 13 cents per gallon, an excise tax of 7 cents per gallon for a total of 60 cents per gallon. That is what the farmers of Canada pay to the federal coffers in order to produce food for Canada and a hungry world.
On January 31, 1980 the minister stated very clearly:
Fuels used in farm production will be exempt from any excise tax and a special price structure established.
You and 1 know that has not happened, Mr. Speaker. This is one of those clear incidents that create a degree of cynicism regarding the Government of Canada and a lack of confidence in the country because the government cannot be trusted. It says one thing and does another. That is a promise it knows very well it could not fulfil.
1 followed that question up in the House today by putting to the minister the promise made in the speech of January 31, 1980, as reported in the London Free Press when speaking to a crowd of 300 in the community of Alvinston, Ontario. At that time he said that the farmers' cost of production would be held in check. As a matter of fact, he pledged to keep farm production costs down. Today I asked him whether he felt he had fulfilled that election campaign commitment.
During the period of time the Minister has presided as the recycled Minister of Agriculture, interest rates have doubled, fuel prices have doubled, pesticide prices have increased by 30 per cent; he is now a member of a government which is proposing an increase in grain freight rates of 45 per cent in three years, to double in five years and triple in ten years while the price of farm commodities goes down. Does he really feel in all honesty and sincerity that he has fulfilled that promise? Well, this was his answer, Mr. Speaker:
-I do not know what research the hon. member is using for all those statements that 1 made because if he is reading speeches I gave during the election campaign, those were not prepared.
What are we supposed to draw from that? Does it mean that when the Minister of Agriculture speaks from a prepared text
Adjournment Debate
he is to be believed, but when he speaks "off the cuff' as he said, in the heat of debate, one should not believe him?
I raise this question at this particular time because I think it deserves an explanation, and I intend to pursue further the commitments and election promises and pledges the minister advanced during the course of the campaign. In all fairness, being a fair person, 1 think it is only fair and reasonable that 1 ask the minister or his spokesman to respond to the government's failure and his failure to produce results. The fact of the matter is that if he cannot produce and fulfil the election promises and commitments he made, he should do one very honourable thing; resign.

NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-EFFECT ON INVESTMENT. (B) DEVELOPMENT OF OIL SANDS IN NORTHEASTERN ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today during question period 1 directed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). I stated that the world investment community does not now consider Canada a safe

July 19, 1982
Adjournment Debate
place to invest. This is due mainly to the national energy policy of the minister. I said that the policy itself is causing an outflow of investment capital at an unprecedented rate, causing a massive run on our dollar which is translating into astronomically high interest rates, which again translates into business recession and massive unemployment. What is the minister going to do to get the confidence of the investment community back? The minister replied verbatim: "1 can't be held responsible for that member's nightmares." The nightmare is a Canadian nightmare.
The number of Canadians unemployed has reached 1.5 million. Right across this country Canadians are losing their jobs. Canadians are losing their farms because they trust this government. Canadians are losing their businesses and their life savings. All of these tragedies translate into child abuse, family breakup, child beating and wife beating, all because of the nightmares people have.
The world investment community does not consider Canada as a safe place to invest, and we can trace that fact back to the National Energy Program.
When the National Energy Program was introduced with Canadian investment dollars, Canadians saw a government with a policy that actually stole from the companies. With its back-in provision it actually moved in on companies and said to them, "We really own 25 per cent." People saw this massive grab by the government with more government involvement. As a result, they moved investment capital out of the country. This investment capital kept the country moving.
That move forced the government to borrow or to attract money from offshore. To do that, the government had to raise interest rates. Immediately interest rates were raised, what happened? The small-business men, the farmer, the man buying a home with his life savings or the man rolling his mortgage into a new mortgage found he had to pay 20 per cent on his money, and all because the government introduced the national energy policy. This was an interventionist policy, to the greatest degree, into an area of the economy which was the one healthy area of Canada. Virtually every economist in Canada stated emphatically the oil industry was the one bright hope on Canada's horizon which could lead us out of this economic stalemate and depression. But the government's policy translated into high interest rates.
If investment money was now flowing into Canada, as it would be under a Conservative government, for development purposes, interest rates would go down. We would not have to raise our interest rates artificially in order to attract funds into Canada to do those things that must be done. We would have business expansion which would cause unemployment to go down. People would be working right across the country. Our megaprojects would be proceeding and we would have the industrial heartland of Canada, Ontario and Quebec, humming. There would be no unemployment and there would be no nightmare. We would not have the nightmare the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources created.
